subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF TASK FORCE ON STRUCTURE OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter Gordon (President of the Privy Council):
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF TASK FORCE ON STRUCTURE OF CANADIAN INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table copies, in English and in French of a report to the government of the task force which was set up a year ago to assist the government in examining the structure of Canadian industry with special reference to foreign ownership and control. The government has decided to release the report at this time instead of using it, as originally intended, as the basis for a white paper which would take some months to prepare. Publication of the report now should assist public discussion of this important subject.
The report is being made public as an expression of the views of the members of the task force and not those of the government. The government will undoubtedly find the work done so competently by the task force of great value and assistance as it pursues its own examination of this whole question, but the tabling of the report does not imply that the government concurs in it or has yet taken decisions regarding its specific recommendations. However, the government will be giving serious consideration to the proposals and views of the task force.
It is the intention of the government to refer the report to the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs so that witnesses can be called and parliament given the benefit of the views and opinions of the many groups in the country which have an interest in this subject.
Certain of the proposals of the task force deal with subjects which are also under study elsewhere in the government. For instance, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is considering amendments to the Canada Corporations Act and the Bankruptcy Act, and is examining various aspects of securities regulations. There is also a reference to the Economic Council of Canada on the Combines Act and on patents, copyrights and trade marks.
Finally, on behalf of the government I should like to thank Professor Watkins, the head of the task force, and his colleagues for their services to the public in the preparation of this report. It will prove to be a valuable contribution to greater public consideration of these complex and many sided issues. I beg leave, Mr. Speaker, to table the report of the task force on the structure of Canadian industry.

[Editor's note: The answer above referred to is as follows.]
There are two reasons why the guaranteed supplement was not paid in January 1968 to certain old age security pensioners:
1. The law requires that a new application for the supplement be made each year since the amount of the supplement is based on the income of the pensioner in the preceding year. Accordingly application forms were mailed on January 2, 1968 to pensioners who received a supplement in 1967. In order that payment of the supplement not be interrupted

February 15, 1968
Inquiries of the Ministry pending the receipt and processing of the application for any year, provision is made in the legislation that payment may be continued for up to four months in that year provided the pensioner notified the minister by December 31 of the previous year of his intent to apply for the supplement in the succeeding year.
At the beginning of November 1967 a form to be signed and used for such notification was sent to all recipients of a supplement. In December a follow-up letter was sent to the relatively few persons who had not returned the notice of intent. In those cases where the notice was not received by December 31, 1967, no supplement could be paid in January 1968 unless the new application was received and processed before the January cheques were printed, and no supplement can be paid for subsequent months until the new application is received and processed. Retroactive payment may be made at that time.
2. A large number of persons became old age security pensioners for the first time in January 1968 when the eligible age for the pension was reduced from 68 years to 67 years. On January 2, 1968, such persons were sent an application form for the guaranteed income supplement. If that application was not returned and processed prior to the date on which the January pension cheques were printed, the pensioner could not be paid the supplement for that month. Applications in such cases when received, will be processed and, where he is found eligible for the supplement, the pensioner will be paid same effective January 1968 in a subsequent month.

As the result of a move by the government and the Bank of Canada to deal with the balance of payments problem the bank rate has gone up to 7 per cent. This is having a negative effect with regard to the domestic economy. It is in part a legacy of arrangements that were made by the minister's predecessor during a disastrous period of office in which Canada was caught by the interest equalization proposals of the United States. Those proposals were, in effect, retaliation for some rather foolhardy proposals put forward by the present government in 1963 and 1964. The ripples from this disaster will come to shore for many years, and this is one more of those ripples.
Corporations are faced with problems of liquidity and working capital. On the one hand the government is saying, it will make it more expensive for you to operate. After all, it was only this week that the banks again, quite naturally in view of the action by the Bank of Canada, moved their prime rate up to 7 per cent. This action was expected to follow as night follows day. If the bank rate should go to 7J per cent, and there is a suggestion this might happen because the steps the government has taken with regard to the encouragement of foreign investment in Canada are not paying off at the hoped for rate, then one might expect that within the next few days after the event the chartered banks would increase their prime rate. This is the way the economy is tied together at the present time.
After all, the corporations provide the backbone of business activity in this country. I do not have the same views about the word "corporation" as do hon. members to my left. They believe that as soon as two people in

February 15, 1968
Income Tax Act
business form a corporation they become big, bad wolves. The word "corporation" covers any company in a business operation, from two or more people to the largest enterprises. They are all corporations. They all pay their income taxes on the same scale. This new section 50 will require the two-man operation, perhaps a husband and wife, to pay their taxes on the same basis as, say, General Motors of Canada, the Canada Cement Corporation or any other large corporation which in most instances has adequate sources of working capital.
The Income Tax Act is now going to make sure that the majority of the medium-sized and smaller incorporated businesses will be right up against the collar of cash requirements all the time. But somehow they will have to find the cash, notwithstanding the fact their working capital may be tied up in inventory or in receivables. The Income Tax Act says they will have to pay one-twelfth of their estimated taxes each month and will have to clean up the balance within three months of the end of the fiscal year. Individuals are allowed four months in which to pay their taxes but corporations will be allowed only three months. The corporation may happen to be a service station operator and his wife who have incorporated the business, or two men operating a trucking service who have incorporated. This is precisely what they are going to have to do.
I suggest that this provision results from the desire of the government for money. It is not anti-inflationary in any way at all. The purpose of the change is to bring in some money quickly in order to cut down the swollen deficit of this administration. Up until this moment I have not been able to ascertain the additional funds the government will get within the next 18 months or two years as a result of this provision, but I would say it is just as nefarious and perhaps even more pernicious in so far as the Canadian economy is concerned than the 5 per cent surcharge on income tax. I will have something to say about the surcharge on personal income tax when we reach clause 5.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
This is an acceleration of the payment of income tax by incorporated businesses. It is an attempt to siphon off more money. Is this for an anti-inflationary purpose, Mr. Chairman? I suggest to the minister that it is not. Taxation is used for the purpose of combating inflation, to eliminate funds that are chasing

too few goods and services. But would anybody suggest that in this country today there are too few goods or services available? Certainly there are not. If we reduce the demand for goods and services in this country, this will bring about, first of all, unemployment as a result of fewer services and a decline in the production of goods that are produced in Canada for Canadians. This again will lead to further unemployment.
It is all right to impose taxes as a means of combating inflation or inflationary pressure in time of war, when we all know that it is desirable not to produce certain goods and engage in certain services because others have higher priority. But income in the hands of the populace as a whole which is chasing too few or fewer goods and services tends to drive up prices. That is classical economic theory, and we do not need to go into the details of the theory of supply and demand in this debate. In this day and age, however, such theory is not applicable. I suggest that in fact the very converse situation will occur. I am wondering whether this is part and parcel of the minister's expressed intention, on behalf of the government, to bring about a little slackness in certain sectors, a slackness that might be tolerated and even encouraged.
What will be the result of some of these consequences, Mr. Chairman? These consequences flow not only from this acceleration of the payment of corporate income tax, which will make things more difficult for businesses, but also for the surcharge on personal income tax. We realize that the government does face certain problems. There is relatively galloping inflation. For example, there is an increase of 4.5 per cent in the cost of goods and services, according to the consumer price index last month. There may have been a couple of years during the early fifties when higher rates of inflation occurred, and we know what the consequences were of that.
This administration also faces the problem of balance of payments on international account. Recently there was the beginning of a run on the dollar owing to a lack of confidence in the international money market. At that time the government had to take steps to reduce its expenditures, put its own financial house in order and take measures to combat inflation. Since the budget there has been a greater increase of inflationary pressure in that some of the new excise taxes are reflected in the cost of living index. And before long, Mr. Chairman, I suggest to the minister
February 15. 1968

that the income tax surcharge will also result in a further increase in the cost of living. This will be due to demands for higher wages. After all, Mr. Chairman, practically every individual who is paid a salary or a wage today has income tax deducted at source. What he is interested in is his take-home pay. Even when he is being paid $250 a week, if $75 income tax is deducted, and now the minister proposes to deduct a further $5 or $10, this individual will be interested in maintaining the status quo and will consequently seek to recover that extra $5 or $10. He too wants to hedge his future against inflation, which is quite a natural reaction.
The government also needs more funds to meet its program of expenditure. I think we could suggest that in certain areas this program could be cut back, but let us just look at some of the remedies that the government proposes to take. For example, Mr. Chairman, as a result of pressure the government stated that it would cut back on expenditure, and with the greatest of fanfare introduced estimates a week ago totalling $10.3 billion. The government stated that this was but a 3.6 per cent increase over last year. However, when we compare estimates with estimates it is, as the Leader of the Opposition rightly pointed out the other day, an actual increase over last year of about 8 per cent. This, Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding the protestations of the President of the Treasury Board who said: "Oh, well, you are really not comparing the same things. Since we are now using computers we can guarantee fewer supplementary estimates this year."
Even if we make some adjustment and include some of last year's supplementaries with the main estimates, which would make the situation more comparable according to the President of the Treasury Board, the increase amounts to about 6 per cent. In actual fact I suggest this 3.6 per cent figure was a big sell-out. Unfortunately many of the communications media bought it and we saw big black headlines declaring, almost as though a miracle had occurred, that the government was holding itself to an increase in expenditure of 3.6 per cent. Of course, Mr. Chairman, that is nonsense; there will be further supplementary estimates. It is just as though I were saying to my neighbour, Mr. Chairman, that I owe him $100 but this does not take into account the $25 I lost to him last night at poker and other liabilities that I have.

We know that there is going to be a further item in connection with the Expo deficit. We are not quarrelling with this at the present time but we do say to the government: Do not tell us that you are going to keep your expenditures within 3.6 per cent of last year's. That was an exercise in misleading the public completely. Then for the government to say that the public service would be limited to an increase of only 5,000 persons a year as against the normal increase of 15,000 a year is to camouflage the matter. The increase has been 15,000 a year only since this administration has been in power. We have had a fantastic increase in the numbers of high-priced jobs in the civil service, but that matter may be gone into on another occasion.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Yet there is not a penny in all these estimates to take care of civil servants who retired many years ago and who today, as the result of inflationary pressures and increased taxes, are facing truly difficult times. As a matter of fact one might say that this government espouses increases for the rich and decreases for the poor. That has been one part of this government's policy, especially as it applies to the public service.
It was strongly suggested to the government that it should set aside some of its more expensive programs. I shall not go into the arguments which were advanced the other day by the Leader of the Opposition about the implementation of medicare but I endorse those arguments wholeheartedly.
With regard to the wise counsel which the Minister of Finance gave to the provinces and municipalities to cut back their spending and save money, may I say that I agree with the minister and support him in those pressures that he is putting on the provinces and municipalities. Some provinces and municipalities have taken heed of that counsel. Over the years some of them have become very fat and lax, I think, in the matter of watching their expenses.
Now we come to the options which are open to the minister. I have spoken about what I think is the inequity and wrong usage of the income tax surcharge. It may be antiinflationary but certainly it hits every wage earner today who comes within a taxable bracket. Surely the minister could have mitigated inflationary pressures by giving private taxpayers the same consideration he gave the corporations some time ago when there was a

Income Tax Act
refundable surcharge, assuming that there was a necessity for any increase in personal income tax. I do not think there was any such necessity. I do not think the government needed to increase personal income tax and I do not think it should have entered the corporation income tax field either.
I have previously expressed myself about excise taxes and about the relative luxuries of tobacco and liquor. Only now, having allowed the provinces complete liberty in this field, has the government of Canada seen fit to move into it. The provinces had complete liberty so far as liquor was concerned to increase revenue without resorting to their legislatures. They merely ordered an increase in liquor prices. Those remarks do not apply to tobacco since provinces must take legislative action to impose an additional tax on tobacco. In any event, I think the populace generally is prepared to accept taxes on these two important items and might have accepted more. I am certain that the minister might have looked toward an extension of excise taxes on certain services as a result of which there would have perhaps been greater equity. In any event, I feel that the acceleration of the payment of corporation taxes which the minister has proposed is a retrograde step.
I hope that in the estimates and in the budget for the forthcoming year these matters will be considered. I am not sure that the present minister will deliver that budget; that question is in suspense at present. I think he would prefer not to have to deliver it, because if he does his hopes with regard to something else will go by the board. In any event, I think the provision I have mentioned is a retrograde step, and the next provision of the bill is even more repugnant to me. I believe that these two steps with regard to income tax are not necessary in any way.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset I must say that it is impossible for me to be enthusiastic about this bill for a number of reasons. The first reason is obvious. No one likes higher taxes. Not many, and no doubt this includes the Minister of Finance, can react as philosophically to paying taxes as Oliver Wendell Holmes who said that paying taxes did not bother him since they were simply the way that he helped to pay for civilization.
There are fundamental reasons for condemning this bill which are to be found when we look at the state of our economy and at the

state of our tax laws generally. Unlike the minister, I have no professional expertise in the fields of fiscal and monetary management. I have never really participated in any previous debate having to do with a review of the Canadian economy or the budget, the reason being, as I have said, that I have not the expertise that the minister and such hon. members as those representing Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, Waterloo South and Edmonton West have in this field. They have repeatedly taken part in debates of this kind. Like many Canadians, in the field of economic and fiscal matters I am an amateur in the general and original meaning of the word.
I have followed with keen interest the policies of the government and its attempts to manage the Canadian economy fiscally and monetarily. This bill amends some aspects of our tax laws. I am not enthusiastic about it because it seeks to amend a tax law that has been condemned, after long and painstaking study on the part of the Carter commission, as inequitable. There can be no more damning indictment of a taxation system than is contained in the verdict of that single word "inequitable", a verdict arrived at by the Carter commission. Not only has the government failed to give any clear indication of where it stands relative to the main recommendations of the Carter report but it has also failed to indicate whether it will even bring forward a white paper or a position paper setting forth government thinking in connection with these proposals so that hon. members can begin to understand what the government has in mind by way of tax reforms.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
This is why many of us approach the bill before us with a negative attitude right from the start. We are continuing to use a tax system riddled with loopholes and anomalies brought about by tax deductions and concessions which discriminate against those who earn their income and favour those who acquire it by way of capital gains. In short, our tax laws continue to be basically inequitable. They allow for the deduction of all kinds of expenses incurred by corporations, including not only such necessary items as office equipment, fuel and so on but also such things as luncheon expenses and the cost of hunting lodges. You name it, and it is likely to be deductible somehow. I am sure the minister is aware that the late President Kennedy made a serious attempt to get the United
February 15, 1968

States Congress to agree to tax reforms to cut down expense account living which is becoming a way of life among a certain element in society. If I may speak in the Jeffersonian idiom for just a moment, I should like to say that our present tax law in connection with expense account deductions appeals to the baser instincts of man and cultivates such instincts.
Our present tax law is inequitable because it tends to profit a few people greatly while discriminating against the many. This can be seen simply by looking at the way in which certain elements in our society reacted to the recommendations of the Carter commission. Through their briefs and their tax counsel they got their message over very quickly. They were opposed in essence to what the commission recommended. These people and their spokesmen were articulate, influential and powerful. They have succeeded in petrifying the government into inaction even to the extent that it refuses to give any indication of its attitude toward the basic proposals contained in the report.
The really sad thing is that hundreds of thousands of Canadians, the majority, in fact, who would receive more equitable treatment if our tax laws were reformed were led to believe by reason of these submissions and subsequent publicity in the press and elsewhere that they would somehow suffer a disadvantage ultimately if the principal proposals in the Carter report were accepted. I believe a hoax of epic proportions has been perpetrated on the Canadian people by those who submitted briefs almost completely in opposition to the major recommendations of the commission. The result is that the government has been paralysed by fear.
Throughout the past three years private bills have been brought forward seeking changes in the income tax law to allow for the deduction of expenses by men and women who in the ordinary course of their employment must incur expense in order to acquire special clothing or tools necessary to carry out their work. This is a simple proposition and one which is fair in every respect. My hon. friend from Sudbury has spoken eloquently about the need for bringing about a change in our present tax law which would make this possible. If this law is to be around for a few years yet, and it looks as though it will be, let us at least remove from it the more objectionable of its provisions.
Income Tax Act
Among these must be considered the nondeductibility of the cost of clothing, equipment and tools used by people in the ordinary course of their employment. Up to the present there has been no indication on the part of the government that it is prepared to accept arguments that such expenses should be deductible, and the basic unfairness of the law continues. Deductions in respect of such items as safety boots, hard hats and tools are not allowed, though deductions for entertainment, recreation facilities for clients and so on are allowed. It is hard to imagine how such a situation could be allowed to continue.
Instead of a proposition to remove some of this basic unfairness we have before us now a proposal to levy a miserable 5 per cent surtax on existing income tax. The minister has presumably taken this course because he feels it is an anti-inflationary measure. If it is an anti-inflationary measure it must somehow dampen consumer demands. But when my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands spoke on this subject last November he pointed out that the present inflation syndrome does not have the characteristics of ordinary inflation. The minister said he agreed, and I think both hon. gentlemen are correct. It is not the kind of inflation with which we have been so familiar in the past.
If the bill before us does dampen demand to some extent it will be operating as though we had the kind of inflation which the minister himself has consistently maintained we are not experiencing. Thus it is difficult to see any logical basis for the course the government is taking. There would indeed be some logic attached to it if prices were rising as a result of excessive demand. But it is generally agreed we are not experiencing this kind of inflation. If anything, this is a cost push, a form of inflation with which we have been unfamiliar during the past few years. If anything the tax increase proposed here is ill suited for the purpose of combating it and will simply aggravate the inflationary trend. How can it avoid adding further to the factory cost of goods produced? It will give a further push to the inflationary factors which are at work. Perhaps this bill is simply a way whereby the government can raise revenue, but it has nothing to do with counter-cyclical management of the economy. As I have already tried to say, it will act perversely on the inflation we are facing.

There are many other major problem areas deriving from the government's policies, equivocation and indecision. Obviously rising costs must have some connection with misdirected fiscal policy and with drifting monetary policy. Since I became a member of the house parliament was persuaded to amend the banking legislation and remove the ceiling on interest rates. We were given some very persuasive reasons for taking that course of action but looking back in retrospect, with hindsight, it is quite clear that the reasons we were given were entirely spurious and it was quite wrong for parliament to take that course of action on the recommendation of the government. The government's advice was wrong. One of the main arguments put forward in favour of removing the ceiling on interest rates was that it would help check the growth of near-banks and other undesirable forms of lending institutions. That seemed like a powerful enough argument, but there were other ways to take care of that problem. In the meantime the cure has been shown to be quite disastrous, with a round of increases in the cost of money to all productive sectors of our economy.
The minister now comes before us with a bill that will have the effect of dampening demand. The government is looking on with equanimity as unemployment passes the 4 per cent mark. This measure will not have a remedial effect in any case because a cost-push inflation requires a different kind of surgery from that which the government seems prepared to undertake. Some of the basic economic problems that tend to aggravate the inflation problem require more major surgery than the government is prepared to undertake.
Quite often we are told about the importance of attracting foreign capital to Canada. Yet in recent weeks we have seen the development of a phenomenon in which Canadian investment capital in the form of mutual funds is flowing southward at a rate which shows a ratio of about three to one in investment by those funds in the United States compard with their investment in Canada.
A few days ago the minister was asked a question in the house about this matter, and the posture he adopted was that this was simply part of the ordinary transaction of business, part of the ordinary movement of capital, and the government contemplated no

special measures with regard to this development. If Canadian investment moneys are flowing across the border at the rate recorded in recent months the question should be asked, is it simply a case of capital seeking a higher return elsewhere? Is that the main reason? Or could it be due to the relative shortage in this country of stock offerings in Canadian enterprises? Is it the practice of Canadian subsidiaries of foreign parent firms to make available significantly large blocks of shares to Canadian investors or Canadian investment funds? When there is an outflow of investment funds to another country it may well be due to the relative non-availability of equity stock in Canada and is not so much a matter of looking for a higher return. It should certainly be within the power of the government to react to this kind of problem and try to do something about it. My colleague from Waterloo South will have something more substantial to say in a little while about the availability of equity stocks in Canada.
The rising cost of housing has been a persistent problem within our economy. The cost has been surging for the past two years and more. All the time the government has been dithering. I use that word deliberately because while we have heard ministerial statement upon ministerial statement we have heard nothing of substance that would come to grips with the essential part of the problem.
Land speculation in urban centres and on the periphery of urban growth centres is a major part of the problem. This is becoming a social evil and not just an economic problem. I realize and admit quite readily that one course of remedial action does not involve federal power but has to do with provincial and municipal powers. Our provincial and municipal authorities should be showing a little more curiosity about how this problem is being dealt with in other places.
I understand that in the state of New Jersey and in other states within the last two or three years a real property assessment law has been devised that seems to go a long way toward dealing with the problem of land speculation which has caused the escalation of land prices in and around urban centres. Since the matter does not involve federal jurisdiction I hesitate to try to describe the nature of the changes that have been made in New Jersey in its real property law whereby
February 15, 1968

there is no incentive whatever for speculators to get into the act. Property taxation is based on land use and productivity to resident users. At the time that such land passes from primary production use, or whatever its use, to commercial development it is taxed retroactively for two or three years. As a result those who own land on the periphery of cities are able to retain it without suffering confiscatory penalties. They hold on to it longer and when it is passed on to commercial developers it is likely that the commercial developer will not hold on to it for one or two years before actually developing it. I believe that such a method of approach, which contains an incentive, would prevent a speculator getting in on the act.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The other factor which bears directly on the problem of escalating costs in housing construction is one that relates directly to this government. It is indeed a matter of exclusive federal jurisdiction. I am referring to interest rates, the cost of money and the availability of funds for housing. The response of the government over the past months and last few years has been to act as though, while possessing sovereign powers, it cannot find any means to deal with the problem of high cost money and relative nonavailability of mortgage funds.
The National Housing Act interest rate has been increased again in the hope that this will encourage the investment of more money in this field. While on the one hand it may have this effect it also has the effect of pushing up the price to such an extent that housing is simply beyond the reach of the majority of potential home owners. When that point is reached any kind of action that is taken becomes irrational. For the majority of the people in this country who are interested in and need housing the National Housing Act interest rate now is already such that it is of only theoretical concern to them. As we go on from day to day and from week to week we find that the National Housing Act interest rate has increased once again, the bank rate has increased and the prime lending rate has increased.
It is surprising to note the rapidity with which one bank follows another in increasing the prime lending rate. This almost gives one cause to wonder whether it might be of some value to have the anti-combines people look into the operations of the banks when they take concerted action such as this. I realize
Income Tax Act
that the anti-combines legislation was never intended to be used in respect of banking operations or at least the operations of the chartered banks. However, it would be more than just an academic exercise for the anticombines people if they were to interest themselves in the operations of our banks and study the way in which it just happens that an increase in the prime lending rate by one bank leads so quickly to a similar increase by the others. In a sense I am rather sad that I allowed myself to be persuaded to go along with the legislation last year which eased the limitations governing the banks in respect of interest rates. Since then there has been a chain reaction of escalation always upward.
There is another matter which I should like to discuss very briefly. It has to do with housing and the problems with regard to residential construction. One of the minister's colleagues, the Minister of Transport, on a number of occasions has advocated the concept of the building of satellite cities. I do not have too much to say in that regard except that I believe this sort of thing will have more and more merit in the years ahead. I do not intend to be offensive to the minister but perhaps the fact that this idea is being proposed by one of his rivals for the leadership may tend to make him somewhat less enthusiastic about it. There has been such pressure on the metropolitan areas in terms of land and land prices that I believe any action which can be undertaken by government to reduce this pressure would be beneficial. For example, the Department of Industry now has a program to encourage the decentralization of industry in this country.

suggestion, Mr. Chairman, it is my understanding that at the request of the minister we did not make general comments on clause 1 but are making them on this clause. This obviously was the attitude taken by the hon. member for Edmonton West. With your indulgence I should like to conclude by saying that at this time, when we are talking

I had intended to make some reference to the efficacy of this cost-push influence and the establishment of a prices review board advocated by my colleagues in past months. I will refrain from doing so at this time, but I should like to point out to the minister that he should prevail on his colleagues in the cabinet to look seriously and closely at the savings of several million dollars which can be made by withdrawing our forces in Europe under the NATO command. I do not wish that comment to be taken as an indication that we are advocating a change in Canada's commitment. At this time, when the United States is lowering its commitment to NATO and Britain is reducing the strength of its armed forces, I think we should have regard to the necessity of maintaining our air squadrons for an indefinite period of time. Tuesday the Canadian Labour Congress presented a brief to the cabinet and yesterday members of the C.N.T.U. made a submission. On one important aspect of policy they were in agreement. They asked the government to cut down favouritism in respect of tax laws. The C.L.C. stated that it has been a long time since a government has shown a propensity to satisfy the wishes of the rich and the powerful equal to that shown by this government. The C.N.T.U. may not have used the same words but the same message was clear. I agree wholeheartedly with both organizations.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the last speaker a question. He mentioned that we do not have ordinary inflation. I agree with him. We do have a price-wage spiral. Is it correct that the major surgery he suggests would be similar to what is taking place in the United Kingdom, that is, a ceiling on wages, prices and profits?

I realize the question is not intended to embarrass me and I will try to answer it. If the government lets things go too far and for too long it may be necessary, in order to cope with a crisis, to impose that type of limitation on prices, wages and

profits. However, when such a crisis is building up it seems logical, since we have review processes through collective bargaining, to maintain a price review. If that is not enough, then the next step obviously must be one of limitations.

The hon. member apparently supports the philosophy of the Carter report. He believes that if a man invests $10,000 and receives $800 interest he should be taxed but if he puts $10,000 into a house he should also be taxed to the extent of $800.1 do not understand that.
The hon. member and I have had some very interesting discussions at lunch-time and I am sure we will have more very soon.

At that time final tax payments had to be made within five months. I understand this period has now been decreased to three months but that the actual tax return must still be filed within six months following the end of the fiscal year.

Mr. Chairman, Bill No. C-193 is a result of the introduction of the mini-budget by the minister on November 30 last. One of the objects of the mini-budget was stated in the first paragraph of the minister's speech wherein he said:
-first, to restrain the inflationary increases in prices, costs and the cost of living-

February 15, 1968

I believe it is a well known tact, one that is accepted by the establishment, that when the economy becomes overheated it needs a little grease. The budget indicated that, as in the past, the way in which an economy is greased is by allowing unemployment to rise. This has been the traditional grease on which our private enterprise economy has functioned for many years. This bill seeks to remove from the consumer certain amounts of money which will, in the minister's words, allow a little slack to take place within the economy. We have interpreted this action, and I believe it is a true interpretation, as being designed to create unemployment and ease the supposed overheating of the economy. The minister has failed to realize that prices can be controlled by other means than reducing consumer income.
Since this statement was made by the minister several matters have been raised in the house. Suggestions have been made to which the minister could have applied his mind. One example is the increase in the price of copper which has taken place since the minister introduced this piece of legislation. It was shown that the profits of the copper corporations, Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company Limited, Noranda Copper and International Nickel Company, were such that the four cent increase per pound in the price of copper was not necessarily required at this time. I fail to see what could be more inflationary in our economy than this increase of four cents per pound in the price of copper.
There is also the case of Bell Telephone Company which increased its profits beyond what was allowed. The rate of profit of this company was set by the house but when Bell Telephone went beyond what had been dictated by the house the government saw fit to introduce a lot of doubletalk to justify these excess profits. The government did this instead of taking action and demanding that Bell Telephone return to the consumers the moneys Bell had stolen from them over the past few years. In the last few days we have also seen an example of profiteering in Canada that has no equal. I refer to the profits being made by Canadian drug manufacturers. The government seems unwilling or unable to deal with this profiteering. I believe it is in this area

speechtext: Order. Perhaps I could ask the hon. member to proceed with his remarks and to confine those remarks to the clause before the committee.

I shall try to abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman. These interjections must not go unanswered, of course, because they would leave wrong impressions on the record. I believe they have to be corrected. I will continue in the vein you have suggested, Mr. Chairman.
I would rather be stuck with our members than yours.

There are a few unruly people here, Mr. Chairman, who do not like to hear the truth. They know that their system is falling apart at the seams and when someone makes constructive proposals all they can do is jeer.
The hon. member for Edmonton West took some pains to defend the corporate cause. He said corporations were going to be hurt a little by this legislation because they will have to make their final tax payments by the end of the third month after the close of the year instead of the fifth month. This is certainly a hardship. There will be no increase in the amount of money they will have to pay. This is just an updating of the due date.
Let us compare the situation of a corporation with that of the average individual. The average individual who is paid by the week pays his taxes within seven days of receiving his money, so the corporation still has a 60-day advantage over the individual taxpayer. I cannot see that it is any hardship on the corporation merely because it has to meet its taxes by the end of the third month instead of the fifth. When the act provided for a five month lag in the payment of taxes this amounted to the government lending corporations money without interest.
The hon. member for Edmonton West said that these corporations will now have to go

out and borrow operating capital. Certainly they will have to go out and borrow operating capital. Why should they use money which rightly belongs to the citizens of Canada? Why should they be able to use this money interest free? If you believe in the free enterprise system then you have to pay what money is worth. Why should these people be unwilling to pay for the capital they use, just as you and I do when we have to go out and borrow capital to meet our operating needs?
There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Chairman, and this fact has been documented within the past four years, that the tax system as we know it today is very unjust. I do not believe that merely patching it up with this type of legislation is going to alter the situation. I believe that the morale of the Canadian people is being lowered by the perpetuation of a system which does not bring equity to the people of Canada in their support of the country through the present tax system.
When Mr. Carter was given the job of studying the tax system he had broad terms of reference. I believe he did a very good job. I was sorry that the minister, in his statement on November 30, more or less rejected the Carter commission report on the flimsy ground that the report was written in 1964 and therefore would not necessarily apply to 1969. I am sure that the figures are going to change between 1964 and 1969 but I feel that principles go on forever. If a principle was right in 1964 I feel quite sure it will be right in 1969. If the principles are wrong now, and I believe they are, they are going to be wrong 100 years from now. I believe we have to take steps to correct these inequities so the people of Canada will have faith in this government which, as you are well aware, Mr. Chairman, is losing the support of the people at an alarming rate. I suggest that the government look at some of the objections that have been made to the Carter recommendations. Almost 100 per cent of the objections comes from the elite of the corporate and monopolistic enterprises, the 2 per cent that controls the Canadian economy. If suggested legislation of that kind is bad for them then it must be good for us. After all, I do not think any legislation could be bad for everybody.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
In their submission to the government these companies condemn any kind of social spending. They care not for the humanities.
February 15, 1968

All they want is to maximize their own profits. Industries that are foreign owned show very little concern for the citizens of Canada. Most of the objections that have been made to the revamping of our tax structure should be rejected by the government on the ground that they are put forward by selfish interests that have no concern for Canada or for the citizens within its boundaries.
The person who bears the brunt of taxation change in this country is the wage earner. His sole source of income is easy to tap because his earnings are known to the minister. So far as the minister is concerned, such a person is naked. He cannot take advantage of any legislation to offset part of his income. He is the man whom the minister is more prone to attack; yet he is least able to pay a 5 per cent surcharge in addition to the tax he normally pays.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to confirm that I indicated to the house that I thought a general discussion could take place most appropriately on clauses 4 and 5. As long as these comments are not repeated on clause 5 I do not think any objection should be taken.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I say that I was in the chair when this agreement was reached. If the committee wishes to have a general debate on a clause other than clause 1 or clause 2, as the case may be, then the Chair would have no objection. However, the Chair does take the view that any comments made by members, even though they may be of a general nature, should relate to clause 4 when clause 4 is before the committee and to clause 5 when clause 5 is being discussed. Perhaps I should invite the hon. member to continue.

Thank you for your indulgence, Mr. Chairman. Clause 4 deals with payment of income tax by corporations and the date of commencement of such payments, so I will confine my remarks to this clause as
Income Tax Act
closely as I can. To my mind corporations have enjoyed a privileged position in our tax structure. They have been treated more like human beings than have human beings themselves. Concessions granted to corporations throughout the years have allowed them to become powerful to the extent that they dominate us economically and apparently politically. More and more legislation seems to be designed to favour those who are in this privileged class and they become more and more privileged.
Let us consider the anomalies within our income tax structure in the development of our natural resources by these corporations. I do not think the minister or any Canadian should be inhibited in his demands for a fair share of the wealth extracted from our natural resources by these corporations. As Canadian citizens we own these resources. There is no doubt in my mind that we should have priority over those who perhaps have their names on a paper. Everything in Canada belongs to the citizens of Canada. Every tree in this country, Mr. Chairman, belongs to you and me collectively. So does every ore body in Canada. It is incumbent upon the minister to extract from corporations that are depleting these resources a fair share of their profit.
It has been shown many times in the past that after mining companies have depleted bodies of ore the taxpayers' money has to be spent on alleviating hardship in the area concerned. Mining companies enjoy a three-year tax holiday. As I said a week or so ago, this law is 40 years old and it is time it was updated to meet the present-day techniques of exploration used by mining companies.
Another anomaly in the tax law of the country is the depletion allowance. The law provides that as the value of an ore body is reduced a mining company can reduce its capital cost by a like amount. However, take the case of the miner who has bought a house in the community. As the value of the ore body is depleted so is the value of this man's home; yet he is not allowed a depletion allowance on his home. This is one area where the minister should have introduced legislation to assist people who take the risk of working and living in a mining community. There is no equity in a system that allows a mining company to depreciate its capital cost at the rate the ore body reduces in value but does not allow home owners to depreciate their properties at the same rate.

[DOT] (5:10 p.ra.)
There are several myths in Canada propagated by the press and various business associations to the effect that too much security will kill initiative. This is interpreted by the minister to mean that we must levy a tax on those we have chosen to be the work horses in the community. If we do not keep them a little hungry and lean they will lose their initiative. If the government were to follow this argument to its logical conclusion it would mean that the government would have to levy a 100 per cent tax on inheritances, since one-fifth of our business leaders inherited their positions. And who are we to say that they have lost their initiative? They still have initiative. Therefore this measure involves a contradiction in principles.

Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he consider that a farm which may have taken a farmer a lifetime of work to acquire should be appropriated by the government through 100 per cent inheritance taxes?

To be clear, Mr. Chairman, I did not propose a 100 per cent inheritance tax. I merely pointed out to the committee that if the argument about incentive were taken to its logical conclusion we would have to introduce a 100 per cent inheritance tax in this country because otherwise we would ruin the incentive of so many people. Surely there is an inconsistency in, on the one hand, keeping the workingman's incentive high by keeping him hungry and, on the other hand, allowing others to live off inheritances. Those who live off inheritances do not have the same inducements as those who have no inheritances. I think the hon. member misinterpreted my intention, as is evident from his question.
The Carter commission made various recommendations to the government and, without being solicited, the mining companies presented some abusive briefs which I believe pushed the government into a corner. The government quickly promised the mining companies that not until 1974 would it consider removing the three-year exemption that the mining companies now enjoy. That shows the degree to which this government is controlled by the corporate elite of this country, that 2 per cent of our population who have the rest of us by the throat.
Had the minister really wanted to do something for Canadians, and I think the Minister

of Finance is the man who can best control the country and best correct many inequities, he would have raised the income tax exemption for our people. The basic exemption of $1,000 for a single person has been in our tax law for goodness knows how many years; it has been there ever since I have been paying taxes. It is completely out of line with present-day needs. I think the exemption for a single man should immediately be raised to $2,000 and for a married man to $4,000, if it is to come anywhere near meeting today's needs.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words on this bill.
It is not always pleasant, not always satisfactory, to Canadians to see their income tax being raised. But I feel that, in the present system, the way we raise taxes is patently unjust. The little man is still going to pay for everything. There is no end to the little man's taxes. He is taxed on all sorts of things: on production and on consumer buying. He is also taxed by the federal and provincial governments, the municipalities and the school boards, to such an extent that he is left with nothing to live on.
Our citizens find it very hard to make a living, especially the poor and those belonging to the middle class. The middle class is now in the process of disappearing, because it is overtaxed. Here in this house, we are unable to administer. We cannot do anything
February 15, 1968

without raising taxes and the rates of interest to financiers.
When the money lords raise their rates, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) does not blame them. One would think that he is pleased when the financiers come and raise their rates on capital, stocks and debentures. Everywhere, this is accepted with open arms.
Bonds are renewed, thus increasing capitalization from $500 to $700 million or any other amount, each time raising the interest rate. Now, those gentlemen have done nothing to receive much more than their capital, while the individual has to work and reduce his own capital. The person who lends his capital sees his income and his capital increase as a result of various increases, including interest rates.
I have here, Mr. Chairman, a table which could make the minister and the hon. members understand.
It is a comparative table for the years 1944 to 1967.
The gross national product amounted to some $11,400 million in 1944, while it reached $62 billion in 1967.
Consumption and expenditures amounted to only $10,120 million in 1944, compared to $40 billion in 1967.
During the same period, capitalization and profits increased from $1,280 million to $22 billion. This means, therefore, that capitalization and profits have increased 17-fold from 1944 to 1967, while the gross national product increased five-fold and consumption and expenditures, four-fold.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, I could also mention the number of cheques in circulation; it went from $60 million in 1944 to $600 million in 1967, that is 10 times more.
Increased capitalization reached, in 1967, $18 billion; yet it seems we do not know where to find the necessary income to finance the various departments and the government administration. Indeed, we do not even touch the capitalization. I am not against capitalization but if, under the present system, capitalization has every right, if it can increase its capital, its rate of interest, I feel the people should have a say. It is imperative to do something for the people, to have a look at their income.
For instance, the banks' assets totalled $6 billion in 1944 and $28 billion in 1967, that is five times more. The stock of 800 large companies was worth $7 billion in 1944 and $102 billion in 1967, that is 14 times more. A Royal
Income Tax Act
Bank share sold for $10 in 1944 and $80 in 1967, that is 8 times more; its dividends amounted to 6 per cent or 60c. in 1944 and to $3 or 30 per cent in 1967, that is five times more.
Everything has increased like that in high finance, in the financial system; while personal income keeps decreasing, that of high finance increases continuously and brings in a hundred times more.
In spite of salary increases, strikes, steps to enable the middle class to live a little better, the opposite always happens; taxes go up and so does the cost of living. There is no end to it; there is no stopping it. High finance always gets the most out of it, because the purchasing power of the citizens is diminished through taxes levied by the federal and the provincial governments, in short by all levels of government.
I feel that the minister should open his eyes and take such a situation into account to avoid an increase in taxes. In the present system, he should take them in capitalization, in the profits on capitalization which are hardly taxed.
It is always the little man that is taxed. Our present system is a system of taxes. If it is impossible to change it, at least let us tax the rich and stop taxing those who have nothing. Let us stop taxing those who do not have enough to live on but let us tax those who have too much. By so doing, everybody will be taxed and everything will turn in circles, everything will come to nothing through too much taxes, the little man will disappear, and when the rich is taxed, he will disappear also. In fact, we will all disappear from earth. With our present system, we will all disappear in the near future. Our system is a system of taxes, increases here and there; in short, it is a system which turns in circles and which, finally, settles nothing, balances nothing. It is a complete, anti-social and antihuman imbalance, and the problem cannot be solved.
We offered you a solution on many occasions; we suggested financing public assets at administration costs, but that has always been refused. We proposed many amendments designed to finance public goods at administration costs, which would have accounted for a savings of $3 billion the first year, but they refused to do that, they closed their eyes and ears, saying: That is a Social Credit theory; we will not consider that.

February 15, 1968
Income Tax Act
On the other hand, where does the minister's theory lead us? Where are we going with this complete imbalance, with this outdated system, with this "anti-arithmetic" system? We cannot go forward, we cannot go very far with such a system, and the minister knows that. If he wishes to do something, for want of solutions better than his own, all he has to do is to come and see us, as we could suggest him some. We have often let him know our solutions, but he refuses to consider them, he refuses to apply them. If the present system continues, we shall soon see revolutions, massacres and general discontent, strikes will multiply and we will not be able to settle any problem.
Our economic system is fundamentally wrong and must be reformed. There is no question of destroying everything, breaking everything down, criticizing everything; it is simply a matter of improving what is wrong. We must keep what is good, but what is wrong must be reformed. That is what we have to say and that is what the minister should do, I think, because it seems to me it would be more logical to do that rather than always increase taxes, in short, rather than always taking away the purchasing power of individuals, who do not have enough already, for the people are suffering from a lack of purchasing power. Proof of this assertion is that we have a $18 billion capitalization in
1967,	and we may have one of $22 billion in
1968,	according to statistics. Mr. Chairman, I believe it is abnormal to capitalize all the time and to deprive citizens of their purchasing power.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 5-Temporary surtax.

Before this clause carries I should like to say one or two words about it. The clause has to do with a surcharge on income tax. It imposes an increase in the personal income tax of people who can ill afford any reduction in their incomes.
I understand the minister will be in my constituency on February 24. Of course I would not know the purpose of his visit, but I think he may find some difficulty while he is there in explaining to the people of Perth why he had to impose this increase in the income tax. It is obvious that it goes back some time. On December 6 I pointed out to the house that this government in its first full

year in office had increased expenditures by 4.6 per cent, that in the following year, 1965, there was an increase of 5 per cent, in 1966 an increase of 7.1 per cent, in 1967 an increase of 13.7 per cent and in 1968 an increase of something like 12 per cent.
In connection with the estimates presented to the house the other day an attempt was made to tell the people of Canada that the increase in expenditures amounted to only 3.6 per cent. However, a correct comparison made with the estimates presented a year ago would show the real increase to be approximately 8 per cent. The President of the Treasury Board did say that because of the use of computers more accurate estimates could be made and there would be no need to ask the house to approve supplementary estimates. I suggest, however, that a cushion of some kind has been included in the figures presented to us and that the computers have not in fact done a true job in estimating likely expenditure.
As hon. members know, the cost of living has been increasing at the rate of some 4.5 per cent a year during the last two years. This simply indicates that the average person in Canada is no longer able to meet these vast government commitments which make it impossible for him to lead the kind of life he is entitled to lead here in Canada.
The inflationary trend which is developing under this government has been admitted by the minister. Indeed, he has attempted to do something about it by means of this tax increase. It has certainly failed to make any impact up to now, according to the most recent figures issued by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. This tax was announced on November 30 and came into effect on January 1, 1968. People have been paying this increase since that date but so far it has done nothing to assist in halting inflation.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The minister has to do something about this matter. Either he or a possible successor will have to bring down another budget almost immediately. The other day when answering a question the minister said that no budget would be introduced before the Liberal convention is held. I can understand that, because we are not going to be around here too much longer. Nevertheless, we should have a budget introduced prior to that convention. A budget will have to be introduced immediately after the Liberal convention to let the people of Canada know where we are
February 15, 1968



going and how we are going to meet the increased estimates which were tabled at the beginning of this week.
The government has been extravagant in the extreme. This has been shown in the way it has disregarded expenditures. It has been shown in the way it has disregarded the people of Canada by increasing taxes. The government has introduced two budgets a year and with each one has taken another bite out of the cherry. I am sure the people of Canada now realize exactly what the government has been doing and how it has been hoodwinking them by claiming they have had prosperous times. Now the whole thing has come home to roost. It is plainly on the government's doorstep. We certainly deplore the imposition of this additional 5 per cent surtax on the income tax of the average Canadian.

Mr. Chairman, I only want to say a few words on clause 3 of Bill No. C-193 now under study. It is wished to insert the following heading in that clause:
Temporary surcharge
I wonder why the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) is not more straight-forward with the Canadian people. Has the minister ever imposed a temporary surcharge or any temporary tax that he has subsequently abolished? It is clear that, in view of the present financial situation in Canada, the minister will not be able to abolish that surcharge he is asking us to approve.
He knows very well that the average Canadian citizen is unable to pay more taxes than at present. He is already paying too much. Even though it is provided that a person must now be paying $100 in income tax to be subject to that surcharge, anyone paying $100 in income tax cannot afford to pay that additional surcharge, and the minister knows it.
Instead of taking the money he needs where it is to be found, the minister always asks the little man to make a sacrifice and to give more. Clause 5 indicates clearly the attitude of the minister and of the present government.
The people are never promised increased taxes or new surcharges during election campaigns. Ho no. In 1963, or in 1965, both sides of the house, Liberals and Conservatives, accused each other of raising taxes too high. They said "Give us the power, and we will reduce taxes". But each time we changed
Income Tax Act
government, taxes were increased instead of diminished.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to do anything in particular about this measure, but I wish to point out that this is the clause that has caused us all a great deal of trouble. Certainly, in its dealings with the Canadian Transport Commission the Bell Telephone Company, as a result of similar wording in the legislation, has had a great deal of difficulty. In brief, this clause will limit the power of the company to invest in other companies. That limitation has brought problems to the Bell Telephone Company and to its subsidiary, Northern Electric.
I think that most people look with sympathy at Bell's problem as it relates to its subsidiary, Northern Electric. Everyone, I think, will agree that Northern Electric has done exceptional work in research and development in order to maintain Bell in a position
IMr. Honey.]
that is envied by other companies across the North American continent. The Canadian Bell company has been able to do things that the United States Bell company has not been able to do, and here I am talking about the various technical systems which are being used in this country. The development of Northern Electric has been helped by the Bell Telephone Company. Northern Electric helps Bell, and Bell helps Northern Electric. They are complementary organizations, so to speak.
One of the problems that faces the government of Canada is the close relationship between Northern Electric and Bell. Since in this country we have private ownership of a public utility and since we have decided that the Canadian Transport Commission shall judge how much the private owner of the public utility shall charge for its services-in short, since there is to be a measure of public control over the public utility-might it not be legitimate to ask Bell to divest itself of Northern Electric? Could not Northern Electric shareholders be given the right to buy all the shares in their company? Surely, it will be only a matter of bookkeeping to establish a separate identity for the company. If the company were independent of Bell there could be no accusation that funds are transferred between the companies or that there is any juggling of any rules or rights.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
On the other hand I believe that much could be gained by Bell if it were to divest itself of a third part, namely the manufacturing end of Northern, which is a large producer of cable and wire and of other facilities on the fringe of telephone operations which are not necessarily part of a telephone complex. It seems to me that this large manufacturing section could be sold to employees, or distributed to shareholders on some basis to which the company would agree. If a stockholder had five shares of Bell it could be decided that he would be given so many shares of Bell, so many shares of Northern, and so many shares in the industrial section of Northern, thus making three separate companies.
While clause 8 may be good for the company it may also add to the problem which hon. members who have read reports of the hearings before the transport commission are aware of, namely that decisions by the board are complicated by the number of companies concerned.
February 15, 1968

I understand that the committee did not go into this matter at any great length, but I raise the problem because I believe it inevitable that some consideration will have to be given to it. As everyone knows, Bell and Northern are a totally integrated operation. Although a financial statement is put out separately for Northern Electric this can be arranged in such a way, and I am not suggesting there is anything dishonest about it, that a greater proportion of expenditures could be made from one pocket than from another, simply because the pockets belong to the same set of shareholders.
In my opinion Bell should seriously consider various methods by which it could divest itself of this type of control, so that its public utility section can be separated from manufacturing and research. If clause 8 as now worded comes into effect Bell's problem will be complicated by any other research it does, or by the acquisition of any other company whose interests do not lie in the telephone field.
If Bell were to buy R.C.A. Victor in order to acquire that company's research facilities, it could end up with a radio and television manufacturing section, and the charge could be made that some of its television production revenue was subsidizing wire which Bell itself uses, R.C.A. Victor then being a totally owned subsidiary of Bell. I do not make an issue of this. I am merely giving advice to the Bell Telephone Company, and saying it will be in trouble with parliament in the future if it does not do something to divest itself of Northern Electric and of any other companies of that type in which it may be interested.
