Mr. Chairman, I will accept your ruling and reluctantly proceed with the remarks I wish to make. What strikes me particularly is the limitation of $600. It does not seem fair to the Canadian taxpayers that people earning under $50,000 should be subject to the surtax and that people earning over $50,000 should be relieved of any further payment over $600. I would have thought that perhaps the Minister of Finance would have
February 15, 1968

been inclined to accept this argument, but he probably finds himself in the unfortunate position of representing the establishment, and finding that it is very difficult to appease them.
Prior to the dinner adjournment I had set forth the proposition that the Minister of Finance found himself in the very unhappy situation of approaching the leadership convention, and having to present to the house Bill No. C-193 which contains the amendments to the Income Tax Act. I pointed out that he really is the author of his own misfortune in that he made a gross miscalculation in his mini-budget of June because he failed to direct the economy and placed too much reliance on the so-called economic tools of fiscal and monetary policy.
I also pointed out that the minister had not given any consideration to the recommendations contained in the Carter commission report. I mentioned in particular that he had been highly critical of the medicare scheme which will become law on July 1. Therefore he now finds himself in the position of being much down the line with regard to gaining the leadership of his party. In his November budget he pointed out that the main culprits in causing a serious economic problem were the cost of living, inflation and the high interest rates. I said that he set forth the usual remedies that the Minister of Finance is so capable of, in striking hard at the workingman and treading easily on the corporations of this country.
With regard to the problem of inflation, it is obvious to most Canadians that whatever steps he has taken have not been very successful in coping with the high cost of living. Even though he recognizes the difference between the traditional inflation of too many dollars chasing too few goods, and the type of inflation that we are suffering from now, which is the cost-push inflation, he seems to pay little heed to the necessity of bringing forth any economic measure that would combat the problem. The striking thing is that the type of cost-push inflation from which we are suffering today strikes hardest at the persons in our society who are most unprotected such as our old age pensioners, the veterans, and persons on fixed income who must pay high prices for food, clothing, maintenance, rent and so on. Yet in the mini-budget he brought forward he did nothing for these people.
The second problem is the matter of the high interest rates. I believe I would be safe 27053-4281
Income Tax Act
in saying that we have the highest interest rates in the history of Canada. From reading yesterday's paper it would appear that the chartered banks of Canada have now raised their prime rates to 7 per cent. We all know that the prevailing rate on Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages under the National Housing Act is 8jj per cent. On conventional mortgages you have an interest rate of 9 or 9J per cent, and it is expected by most Canadians that this interest rate will increase to 10 per cent. That represents the approach taken by this minister regarding high interest rates. When we had the amendments to the Bank Act before us the minister came up with a formula for applying a rate of 11 per cent for a quarterly average on short term Canadian bonds. We studied this in the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. With the help of members of several parties we changed this drastically. We in the New Democratic party now find that prime interest rates are up to 7 per cent.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Not long ago I remember somebody suggesting that an individual who purchased a house for $18,000 with a C.M.H.C. mortgage would eventually pay $42,500 on the basis of an interest rate of 8J per cent. With an interest rate of 8| per cent this cost will increase. If things continue as they are, an individual will soon be paying $50,000 for a $18,000 home. This is what the chartered banks, finance and insurance companies want to prevail in Canada.
The government has failed to take into account the high interest rates which add to the cost of homes. The greatest contribution it has made to the solution of this problem is the initiation of a housing conference, and the resolution now before us to increase the ratio of mortgage loans. At the time the budget was presented, certain members of my party indicated that the basic reasoning behind the minister's budget could be related to an increased unemployment situation as a result of a slowing down in the economy. We now find that prediction to be accurate. Unemployment figures have reached almost 500,000, with a tremendous disparity in the maritime provinces, Quebec and on the west coast. Several hon. members predicted that this situation was bound to occur, following the minister's budget.
The Minister of Finance has ignored some very basic principles in respect of inflation and high interest rates. He has ignored the

February 15, 1968
Income Tax Act
plight of those people who are affected by these rates, and the increased cost of living. Yesterday's newspapers noted that the contribution of the Liberal women of Canada took the form of a recommendation in favour of the rejection of a guaranteed annual income and a negative income tax. That was their best contribution. They also suggested that the tone of parliament should be lifted without giving consideration to the economic problems facing the country today.
The Minister of Finance also ignored other tax resources he could tap to meet certain problems with which we are confronted. He has completely ignored the Carter commission report and the application of its recommendation regarding a capital gains tax. When we talk about capital gains we are not talking about the individual who sells a home for something more than he paid for it, because we know the profit he makes will be absorbed by the price he pays to replace that home. We are talking about those individuals who make vast sums of money on the stock exchange or through major transactions. We think, like Mr. Carter, that these people should be taxed heavily.
The Minister of Finance has also ignored the depletion allowances. As a member who has received a tremendous number of briefs from the resource industries of the country, I am fully aware of the fact that 5 per cent of the population controls this country financially, and that the same 5 per cent are not taxed proportionately as high as the other 95 per cent. This 5 per cent screams the loudest about the Carter commission recommendations, whereas the other 95 per cent would welcome them because they feel a reduction in their taxes would result.
The Minister of Finance has also ignored the life insurance companies so far as taxes are concerned, and has given them preferred treatment, to which they are not entitled. If these companies had been taxed in the ordinary way we would be in a position to more than pay for the medicare scheme going into effect on July 1. Having listened to several speeches of members of the Conservative party, I find it very difficult to distinguish between the philosophy, as presented by their spokesmen, and the philosophy of the Minister of Finance. I listened today to the hon. member for Edmonton West speak on behalf of corporations and the time limitations for payment of corporation taxes. It seems to me that he, along with other members of his

party and the Minister of Finance, has totally ignored the economic planning this country needs to solve its economic problems.
For some time we have advocated the establishment of an investment advisory board to direct the economy of the country, and our investments. The minister has totally ignored his opportunity to direct the investment of the savings of Canadians. The most flagrant example we have had in this regard is the minister's failure to act in a positive way in conjunction with the Canada Development Corporation, which would provide an opportunity for Canadians to invest in Canada. The minister has totally ignored the recommendation of this party to establish a review board which would indicate to the Canadian public the government's interest in offsetting high prices. Such a review board could study the situation, just as trade unions do during the complex process of negotiating increases in wages.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
It is very obvious to us why we are in a state of economic plight today. This is the result of a lack of imagination on the part of the Minister of Finance in coping with today's economic problems. He wants to represent the establishment and he fails to use the new and exciting economic tools which are necessary to combat today's problems. It may be necessary to bring forth new measures to combat these problems. We in the New Democratic party feel that the Minister of Finance is not able to bring forth the proper solutions to these problems.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal with clause 5 which provides for a temporary tax.
That beats everything, Mr. Chairman. If I did not know the minister, I would say that he is naive. What a wonderful expression: temporary tax. Temporary but for how many years?
Temporary, Mr. Chairman, that may mean for the next century of confederation.
It is temporary in order to increase it later.

The hon. member for Mer-cier says that it is temporary in order to increase it later.
This is the heading, Mr. Chairman: "Temporary surtax". Some will believe that it will be for a short time only, but I have never
February IS, 1968

seen a tax already levied that was abolished later. No, once it is levied, it is there to stay.
That is so typical of the present government. They call it temporary to mitigate the blow. Taxes are increased by 5 per cent and that will bring in more revenue to the government, of course.
When I look at the government's estimates for the year ending on March 31, 1969, which the minister tabled not too long ago, I notice items which strike me, among others the interests to be paid by the government on the public debt.
Last year, the interest amounted to $1,273 million.
That is only temporary.

And this year, it amounts to $1,406 million, that is an increase of $133 million during one year. The largest increase in government expenses for next year is the interest on the public debt.
I now come to another item, the following one, that is family allowances. It is quite a considerable increase, Mr. Chairman, since the estimates will rise from $614 to $615 million, that is $1 million next year for all the Canadian children compared with a $133 million increase for a few capitalists.
Well, it is precisely to foot that increased interest on the public debt that the government is now compelled to levy a 5 per cent surtax on personal income. If taxes are increased, it is because money is needed, and if more money is needed, it is precisely because the interest on the debt has gone up. I suggest that the yield of the surcharge will be used to try and balance the budget in order to pay the higher interest on the public debt.
When I was elected to this house in 1962, the first thing I did, when I was first given a copy of the blue book, was to look up how much Canada was paying in interest on the public debt. At that time, the interest stood at $780 million. Six years later, it has reached $1,406 million. While the rate of family allowances has not even increased by 8 per cent, the interest on the public debt has almost doubled in the last six years.
We have come to the point where the interest on the public debt is the second highest expenditure of the federal government, amounting to $1,406 million. The two largest expenditures of the federal government are: first, the amount appropriated to national defence, that is $1,800 million; second, the interest on the public debt, in the amount of
Income Tax Act
$1,406 million, which makes a grand total of $3,200 million.
Mr. Chairman, when I look at those astronomical figures representing the amounts spent on national defence and interests on the public debt, I cannot help telling myself that were Quebec independent, it would save a lot of money on such expenditures since it pays yearly $1 billion in taxes for those two items only. The budget of national defence and the interest on the public debt amount to $3,200 million and the share of Quebec in this expenditure, which is about 30 per cent, amounts to $1 billion a year. Should Quebec withdraw from confederation, it would not contribute any more to these expenditures for national defence and it would leave Ottawa to straighten out its war debt.
That means that Quebec would be, overnight, richer by a billion dollars which, at the present time, is collected in income tax and other taxes and spent absolutely uselessly.
Mr. Chairman, I oppose this temporary tax increase because the budget proves this increase in taxes will be used to pay financiers.
The Canadian people will pay 5 per cent more income tax. And why? Because the interest which the federal government will have to pay next year will be increased by $133 million. This increase in income tax will be used to pay the increase in the interest rates. Had it not been for higher rates of interest, the hon. minister would not have been forced to raise the income tax, and he would have $133 million less to pay in interest on the public debt; but as the interest has gone up, he has had to find the amount of $133 million, and that is why income tax has been raised by 5 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that instead of always digging into the pockets of the low-wage earner for taxes, the hon. minister should revise his system in order to let the little man, the worker, the low-wage earner, keep the money that would enable him to buy Canadian products and benefit a little bit from the wealth of the land.
But the minister prefers to sacrifice the people of Canada to a few financiers who are the only ones to get rich with the new budget and new taxes; these taxes are a tribute to high finance, which has succeeded in obtaining from the minister increases in the interest rates.

February 15, 1968
Income Tax Act
The minister would like to govern the country. Since he is the minister of the Department of Finance, he is perhaps the one most responsible for the increases in the cost of living, the inflation we are having now through the raise in interest rates and the continuous increases in taxes. Now, he would like to govern the country. If the Liberal party puts the leadership of the country into the hands of the minister, I say that the Liberal party will be placing the country in a state of depression and crisis, and I hope the Liberal party will save us from such a catastrophe.
Mr. Chairman, I therefore oppose this raise in taxes, because I realize that it will only be used to pay the higher interest rates demanded by financiers.

I have a very straightforward request to make of the minister tonight, and I hope he will accede to it. I should like to ask him why he does not listen to his speech writer. He seems to have an excellent speech writer, and I am referring in particular to the speech given to the luncheon meeting of the Canadian Club at the Royal York Hotel, Toronto, on January 8. There are some excellent statements in that speech, and I should like to quote some of them:
What can be done? I agree entirely with those who deplore the deliberate creation of unemployment as a means of checking inflation.
Yet, Mr. Chairman, this is what seems to be happening. The budget proposals we have before us seem to be designed to create unemployment. If they were not designed to create unemployment, they seem to be having that effect at any rate. Our rate of unemployment has increased substantially over the past few years, and this is happening at a time when the United States economy is experiencing the lowest level of unemployment within the last five or ten years.
It seems difficult to understand why we should inherit inflation from the United States and yet not inherit the full employment situation as well. In the speech to which I have referred, the minister, or his speech writer, went on to say:
It unquestionably involves new techniques and new attitudes on the part of those who wield market power, both labour and management. The traditional instruments of fiscal and monetary 
policy must be employed with courage and skill, but they are no longer sufficient, in my view, to ensure that desirable combination of prosperity and stability which we all seek.
Those are admirable words. I wish the minister had taken some action to back them up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Does he know who did write those words, both what I uttered and what was written?
No, I am sorry, I do not know the name of the speech writer, but I would be pleased to learn his name if the minister would care to offer that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was the Minister of Finance.

In that case, I congratulate the Minister of Finance and simply say to him: Why don't you listen to what you are saying? This was a very good speech, but I think the minister should pay some attention to his words and back them up with some action. This excellent speech writer, whom I admire, then had this to day:
We must work out a Canadian solution.
I heartily agree with that; this is the very thing we must do. I think perhaps the minister should spend more time looking for a Canadian solution instead of going down to the United States and praying for events there to change. We do need a Canadian solution, and we need it desperately. Up until now we have not had measures proposed that will solve the economic problems of this country. Such measures as have been proposed have involved the old fashioned unproductive bromides. We need new measures. The minister talked about new measures, but we have not seen any of them.
We are faced with a need for increasing our social capital. Even the minister will agree that there is a need for medicare. There is a desperate shortage of housing in this country. We need revenues to correct the disparities between individuals and help raise the level of income. With 20 per cent of our population living in poverty we need to redress the difference between the rich and poor sections of this country. For that purpose we need revenues. However we see no real evidence that the minister understands the problem.
It seems to me a proper course of action for the minister would be to suggest a means of increasing productivity and wealth in this nation. If we did this, we could generate the
February IS, 1968

revenues required lor the kind of society to which we aspire in this country. If we look at our productivity, we realize it is 20 per cent to 30 per cent lower than it need be. Even if we did not close the gap of 20 per cent to 30 per cent, but if we simply increased productivity by 10 per cent we would increase our gross national product by $6 billion. If you calculate that 30 per cent of that increase goes in taxes to the various municipal, federal and provincial governments, there would be another $2 billion available to help the people of this country. This represents a far greater amount than the minister hopes to collect from this 5 per cent surtax.
The minister seems to be making the same mistakes as the previous government made.
Oh no, worse.

I do not know whether they are any worse, but they are certainly not any better. I should like to quote from the report of the Economic Council of Canada which refers to the year 1960. Someone has said that was a bad year. You are right; it was a bad year. Unfortunately this year is not any better. It does not seem to make any difference in this country which one of the old parties forms the government, we wind up with the same results.
I am quoting from the report of the Economic Council of Canada:
For the year 1960, the economy was capable of producing over 8 per cent more production and income than actually occurred. The increases in the major federal tax revenues stemming from an attainment of potential output, however, would have been considerably greater than the implied rise in output itself. It has been calculated that personal income tax yields at the given rates would have been 12 per cent, and the corporation income tax yields by more than one third. In the aggregate such calculations indicate that at potential output levels in 1960, federal tax yields at the rates then in effect would have been over 18 per cent higher than the actual collections in that year when the economy was operating substantially below capacity.
The present minister should have been aware of the kind of problem created when there is slack in the economy. I should like to put on the record a further quotation from David W. Slater, "Economic Policy and Economic Research in Canada since 1960":
But the high unemployment and extremely disappointing productivity experience in this "five year stretch"-
Income Tax Act
The period referred to is between 1958 and 1962.
-still stands out as one of the major failures of Canadian post-war economic performance. Canada's gross national product was at least 8 per cent below potentials during these years. The cumulative five year loss of output would sum to $15 billion, or more, in current prices.
This is a sizeable amount. One would have hoped the present Minister of Finance would have learned from experience when the nation is faced with high levels of unemployment. It is bad enough in the central provinces, but it is much worse in those provinces that seem to suffer most under circumstances of this type. I understand that unemployment levels in the maritimes are somewhere around 11 per cent. This is a catastrophic level for that area. Unfortunately the minister seems prepared only to raise taxes and diminish the gross national product. Then, he moralizes about the need to pay as we go.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Earlier today my colleague from Springfield referred to the banking policy of the government and indicated that he reluctantly supported the policy because of the persuasiveness of the Minister of Finance, who offered some excellent reasons for removing the ceiling on interest rates charged by banks. I recall his assuring the country that setting the level of interest rates was the direct responsibility of the Minister of Finance and that he accepted that responsibility.
I think that tonight he must answer for that responsibility. I remember voicing my concern at the time, Mr. Chairman. As reported at page 7320 of Hansard for July 7, 1966 I said:
If the bank rate in this situation is freed from restriction or permitted to increase, I have no hesitation in saying that Canada will face the highest interest rates, the highest cost of money, in all history.
I also recall some rather unpleasant noises that came from the government benches at the imputation that such a thing would happen. Then later, as reported at page 7321, I said:
To remove the interest ceiling without proper safeguards is to raise the cost of every single thing in this country. It is to put the cost of money in Canada at a height it has never achieved previously, and one that no one at this point can calculate.
I then went on to say that interest rates of 8 and 9 per cent on commercial lending would be possible through this type of

approach, and there were hoots and shouts from government benches, incredulous that interest rates could reach 8 or 9 per cent in this country. That was not very long ago, Mr. Chairman. Now interest rates have not only reached that level, but exceeded it.
The minister has a lot to answer for. He poured oil on the troubled waters. As reported at page 7237 of Hansard, he said:
I should like to re-emphasize the determination of the government that the fresh winds of competition shall permeate our system of banking and finance.
Here I should like to recall to the committee the great aplomb with which the minister on that occasion made this announcement to the nation. He continued:
We are determined that the system shall operate in the interests of the greatest number of Canadian consumers and businessmen. We are determined, in particular, that the interests of the small borrower and the small businessmen shall be protected and furthered.
Perhaps the minister will tell us whether this has eventuated.
We believe that the most effective way to achieve these ends is to encourage and to enforce competition. In this view, the government is supported by the royal commission on banking and finance and by the Economic Council of Canada. If there are many competing sources of loan funds and many institutions freely competing for the custom of the consumer, we are convinced that he cannot help but benefit.
I think that the policy of the minister has proven to be a failure. Perhaps no one should blame the Minister of Finance for this because many of us were persuaded at the time that this approach had a good possibility of succeeding. I do not think there was any conspiracy or any malice on the part of the minister when he made that speech. I think he believed at that time that the removal of the interest ceiling would be beneficial.
However, Mr. Chairman, since it has not, I think the minister will have seriously to consider making an admission that his policy has not worked, whatever the reason for it is. Unless he finds other measures to control the rapidly escalating cost of money in this country he will have to reimpose the ceiling on interest rates. I believe that he or one of his officials assured us that it was quite possible that this would be the case if the measure did not work out as anticipated.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the problem that is ailing the economy is not lack of money. Canada has one of the highest rates of saving in the world. I think almost 20 per

cent of our gross national product goes into savings. It is not that we do not save enough but that we misuse the savings that are at our disposal. We simply spend them wastefully. I sometimes think there is no other country in the world so wasteful with capital as this country of ours. Perhaps we have acquired capital too easily and therefore have not had to conserve it or invest it as well as we should.
I should like to put on record the situation that exists in many of the industries in this country that are over capitalized. These industries have used far more capital than necessary. This is a bad state of affairs and cannot and should not be allowed to continue. The minister must give consideration to taking measures that ensure that the capital and savings at our disposal are used in better fashion than has been the case in the past.
I should like to quote from an article that appeared in Time magazine on February 2, 1968 which carried a statement by Robert Fowler, president of the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, who warned the annual meeting of that association that "growth is fine but an epidemic of elephantiasis could be serious." The article continues:
"It is more than clear that Canadians have made a creditable contribution to their own misfortunes," Fowler told the association. Fowler blamed excessive rivalry between companies eager to get the jump on each other, and between provinces only too happy to offer loans and tax inducements. As a result, he said, "there has been a misuse of public and private capital at a time when capital is scarce. There must be better ways to order our affairs."
I should also like to refer to part of an article written by Ron Grant that appeared in the Gazette on November 8, 1967:
Expansion in the pulp and paper industry has created a situation where companies are reaching into every corner of the world market and sometimes coming up empty-handed. It's no longer a seller's market.
New mills coming onstream in Canada, along with similar expansions in other countries, have resulted in excess capacity, increased depreciation, start-up problems-
One would think, Mr. Chairman, that with all this excess capacity and evidence of competition-and, after all, there should be competition if there is excess capacity-prices should come down. But no, prices are not coming down, and will probably have to go up as manufacturers seek higher mark-ups on their volume of production.

I should like to quote from the Financial Post for July 17, 1967, which had this to say:
In spite of current softness in the pulp market, there is little indication of a general break in price among B.C. companies. "Most of us think it would be a mistake to reduce prices. It would not get us anywhere," one company's spokesman said.
This comment appeared in the Globe and Mail for August 4, 1967:
Despite excess capacity in newsprint, prices have been firm. A $3-a-ton price increase went into effect July 1. Analysts say it is unlikely that the Industry will retreat from the new price level, even if mill operating rates decline further.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, this excess capacity has benefited no one. It has not benefited the pulp companies, it has not benefited the public and it certainly has not benefited the nation.

One of the industries that most glaringly displays a misuse of capital is the oil industry in this country. In Alberta production is rationed out among the various fields, pools and wells. For some years total production was about 45 per cent of capacity but now it has dropped to 37 per cent. At the current rate of production, according to Charles S. Lee, president of the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada, the impact of the Rainbow Lakes discovery could be to reduce this to 25 per cent of capacity. The investment in this industry has been calculated to be somewhere between $7 and $14 billion. We do not know the exact amount because only those in the oil industry can supply the answer. Nevertheless we must again ask how much of this money has been totally wasted? How much of this money, and it is mostly United States capital, have we imported for no good purpose? How much of this money have we brought in simply to pay interest and dividends on unproductive capital? How much better would it have been had the oil industry used the capital it needed, instead of spending the money in this way?
In a recent report by Walter S. Levy, prepared for the Independent Oil Association of Canada, we find this comment:
Nonetheless, there is little doubt but that present relatively low utilization of capacity imposes a heavy cost burden on the Canadian producing industry, which could seriously impinge on exploration incentives if it persists. For Alberta, in particular, production is very much below capacity; the ratio of production to capacity improved from 41 per cent in 1960 to around 47 per cent in 1963 and 1964, but has since declined to under 44 per cent In 1965.

What are we doing with all this oil exploration? Canada now has almost twice the proven reserves of the United States.
Would the hon. member permit a question? What is the source of his last statement about proven reserves?

I shall again read from the report. Referring to Canada it says:
Canada's 1965 ratio of reserves to production of 23 years compares with 12 years in the United States; and
Canada's 1965 ratio of production to productive capacity of 55 per cent compares with 73 per cent in the United States.
In other words, our reserves to production are 23 years, as compared with 12 years in the United States.
Would the hon. member kindly talk about this matter in ratios, and not talk about absolute proven reserves?

The point I am trying to make is that we have explored and created more reserves than we could possibly use in the foreseeable future. There is all kinds of oil lying around that is not being tapped. The tar sands are hardly being touched for fear of what full production from them might do to upset the entire marketing arrangement in Canada.
Nonsense.

I am delighted to see the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources entering this debate. Perhaps he could say something about potash, because it seems that we are doing with potash exactly what we have done with oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: The hon. member cannot have it both ways.

A news report of February 10 of this year says that we have overloaded potash production, just as we have oil production. In other words we have spent more money on this commodity than needed to be spent; we have brought about all kinds of improvements in production and we have no place to put the potash. It seems to me that the industry has jumped far ahead of its sales and markets, and that constitutes a gross misallocation of capital.
The Carter commission is concerned about this factor. Members of this party have spoken of the inequity of our present tax system. They have pointed out how Carter has called for equity in our system of tax allocation. But he made another point also. He said that our present tax system bonuses many industries in this country that do not need bonusing. Not only do they not need to be bonused, but they are bonused for the wrong kinds of production. Our system is not neutral; it distorts the capital markets of this country and other countries and puts money into production efforts that should not be bonused. The report says that we should return to a more neutral tax system. If we believe, truly, that capital has a way of going where it is required, then let us do something about that belief. Let us stop bonusing our primary resource industries. Carter was talking not only about our tax system of bonusing but of depletion allowances, forgiveness grants and tax holidays.
We started off admirably in this country with programs such as the designated areas program, which were to bring industries into certain areas. Nobody quarrels with the aims of such programs, except where they have had bad effects, as evidenced by the electrical industry. For example, recently R.C.A. announced that it would open a $25 million tube plant in a certain area. The government contributed $5 million to that. The news report in my hand says:
The federal Government put up an estimated $5-million toward the cost of the plant under its area development program .. .
Mr. Drury later saw dozens of automated cradles hanging empty because of a drop in the demand for color T.V.

This plant has a capacity to manufacture 300,000 tubes annually, yet demand in Canada only requires 190,000 tubes annually.
Another news report, dated May 9 of last year, says:
A Sylvania official said:
"We are quite concerned at the situation, since sales are about 50 per cent below expectations."
The official was talking about his own plant. He continues:
"Our plant alone could supply the whole of Canada's market at the moment-and there are still the other two manufacturers."
That statement shows that one plant can supply the entire Canadian market. This being so, we must again ask, can we afford to use capital in the way we now use it? Our capital use is tantamount to capital misuse. In the long run we shall derive few benefits. Instead we shall see chaos, which will not be good for our industry, our consumers or our nation.
There is evidence of severe overcapacity in other industries, and particularly in the heavy electrical equipment industry. A news report of February 13 of this year says:
A recent survey of manufacturers of power transformers and allied equipment showed that some companies have spare capacity as high as 40 per cent for later this year and early next year.
The same situation prevails in companies making furniture and in companies making pipes for pipe lines. It applies to refineries, and I could go on enumerating industries.
I should now like to say to the speech writer who wrote about the need for a new approach to Canada, that he should do something about that new approach. He must realize that we cannot go on as we are, using general fiscal and monetary policies alone to regulate our economy. Desirable though fiscal and monetary policies may be, new instruments of regulation must be found. Perhaps he is thinking of some new instruments; if so, he should tell us about them.
Personally, I think we should establish some form of capital priorities board. I do not know what form such board could take, neither am I unaware of the difficulties in creating such a board. But in the light of the evidence of the misuse we have made of capital, especially imported capital. I think we ought to establish such a board.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I think the minister should consider whether the tax benefits now conferred on holders of equities should not be given to the holders
February 15, 1968

of government bonds instead. Let us reward those who are contributing their money to public purposes, rather than to private purposes alone. I think this should be considered, especially in the light of the difficulty in financing government expenditure. Public expenditures are valuable and helpful. In the foreseeable future there will be a great deal for public financing. If we are to depart from neutrality in our tax legislation, let us do so in favour of public expenditures rather than private expenditures.
I believe also, as many speakers from this group have said, that we must have a price review board to examine the changes which are taking place in this field and find out what kind of restraint could be exercised by such a board. Unless we can be given some hope that the government is entertaining ideas along these lines it is impossible for anyone to support the entire, useless and damaging measures contained in this bill.

I should like to put on record one or two thoughts I have in connection with this clause, and to say a few things about the subject under debate at the present time. I bring to this no professional, fiscal or economic expertise and I bring to it no volume of statistics or documents. I bring merely a sincere and steadfast opposition to clause 5 and everything it stands for, and a sincere and steadfast feeling of sympathy with the thousands of people who write to hon. members of this chamber every week of the year asking for some relief from the effects of the critical cost-price-tax juggernaut under which they are crushed at the present time.
I ask the Minister of Finance where he thinks the ordinary people of Canada will find the money to pay this surtax which he proposes to levy. I ask where he thinks the elderly people will find the money to pay this tax. They are hard put now, to keep body and soul together, to keep off the blasts of winter and buy the drugs necessary for their health and well-being. I ask him about the retired people, those living on fixed incomes who have been seeking relief ever since this government was elected, and who have sought it in vain. They asked for relief and help, and what did they get? They found themselves poorer than ever. It was an exercise in total frustration.
The Leader of the Opposition made reference this week to the fact that a very large
Income Tax Act
group of pensioners in this country, those living on federal superannuation payments, is still looking to the government for long overdue assistance. My hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition also drew attention to what he felt was the folly of such government programs as medicare, in the light of the needs which beset many categories of people in this country at the present time. The public service pensioners are only one of the classes who are in need. All pensioners come into this category because all of them need help in coping with the cost of living today.
Who will speak for the widows of this country with children to support, or for all who have limited incomes, limited means of livelihood? When the minister proposes to levy a surtax of this sort, I ask him: Who on the government side has given thought to these classes of people? What about the position of those in the lower income groups? What about the position in which great numbers of wage earners find themselves? Those who are fortunate enough to be in the upper income brackets may be able to pay this surtax without too great difficulty; but these are a minority.
I need not remind anyone of the dire economic stress which a great many Canadian families face today. I am sure the mail of every hon. member is filled with pleas for relief, for some form of escape, for some hope of an improvement in the context of the cost-tax-price squeeze felt by most Canadians, particularly by those in the lower and middle income groups, those on fixed incomes, those on pensions, those who are retired and those who are widows with young children to raise, educate and support.
Who on the government side speaks for these Canadians when the proposal is made to impose an additional financial burden upon them? I do not accept the suggestion which may be made from one corner of this chamber that the socialists speak for them, because members of the N.D.P. have demonstrated in some of their utterances today, if they have not done so before, that they approach this problem only in a doctrinaire manner; their hypothetical panacea for these ills is nothing but a series of superficial arguments based on hoary socialist principles which represent a creed outmoded and outworn, a creed which has never delivered anything by way of progress or constructive prosperity in the marketplace of Canada and which has never, fortunately, had an opportunity to do any

damage of a major nature-and I trust it will never have a chance to do so in the future.
The N.D.P. makes a great pretence of speaking for Canadians in difficulty but they have never been called upon to deliver; they speak from a protective segment of the political scene. They have never had to deliver in the context of the practical difficulties attached to running a country or a government. The hon. member for Waterloo South said it did not seem to make much difference which of the two major parties were in power so far as the financial difficulties of the people was concerned. We all know he was referring to the Conservative party and the Liberal party. I suggest to him it would make a tremendous difference if his party were in office. And the Canadian people know it; and that is why his party has never been in office. I would ask the same hon. member, and those of his colleagues who have spoken in the same theoretical, hypothetical vein, what about the situation in Great Britain where finally the people seem to have come to their senses with respect to the panacea of socialism? I would ask him, what about the situation in Denmark where the people not only seem to have come to their senses but have articulated that fact by throwing out a socialist government?
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The hon. member for Waterloo South presented a typical, classical socialist argument, but it contained the depth and degree of reasoning, and the strength and substantiality of most socialist arguments, that is to say, it was totally flimsy, and collapsed on examination. That was demonstrated by the fact that he was confused by questions directed to him by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare and by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
That party is not speaking for the people in this country who are in financial difficulty at the present time, and I suggest that the minister through the measure he has introduced is not speaking for them either. I ask who is speaking for people who are in these straits? This is the reason why, without any financial, fiscal or economic expertise I have risen to inject my observations into this debate.
The average wage earner in this country, if he has a family to support, has an extremely difficult time meeting his economic needs. You know that, sir, from your mail, as well as I know it from mine, and as well as anybody in this chamber knows it from his or her mail. With the pressure of taxes, living

costs, food costs, all the costs that go to make up the spectrum of survival and existence, the average wage earner has all he can do to keep his head above water. He is asking for some relief, not for an additional burden or penalty such as that exemplified in the measure the minister has introduced.
The difficulties that I refer to do not even begin to take account of the situation with respect to the elderly, the pensioners and all those on fixed incomes. The average wage earner has a difficult enough time, but this does not begin to take account of the extreme hardships of those in the latter three categories I have mentioned, the elderly, the pensioners, and all those on fixed incomes.
This, sir, is a mean and cruel tax. It is hitting at a segment of society already pressed almost to the breaking point. The critical fiscal and financial situation in which these Canadians to whom I refer find themselves, indeed all Canadians find themselves, is not of their own making. They should not be held to account for it, and should not have to find the way to pave the government's avenue of escape out of it. The critical fiscal and financial situation in which the government finds itself is of its own making.
Some 18 months ago the government established a pattern of 30 per cent wage increases when it intervened in three labour disputes and ordered settlements to be made on that basis. That was only one example of fiscal and financial irresponsibility on the part of the government, but it was one of the most graphic. It has continually come back to haunt the government and to hurt Canadians time and time again in the 18 months since then. You cannot go about making outlandish settlements like that without paying the piper, paying the price somewhere down the line. Who is paying the price? It is the average Canadian wage earner, the pensioner, the Canadian in all those categories to which I have referred. He has to meet his grocery bill, his rent bill, his mortgage bill, pay for his children's education, pay for drugs in an effort to stay alive in this economic situation in which all factors seem to be arranged and arrayed against him.
When wage increases of that outrageous size are implemented, and with the rapidity and in the sequence in which they were implemented, they cannot help but have an effect on the marketplace which will militate against the economic well being of all Canadians. They cannot help but have an effect which takes the form of a situation that
February 15, 1968

ignites a further spiral of costs and prices. These settlements could not help but touch oil a new spiral in costs and prices, and could not help but reflect those in the marketplace.
The small wage earner is the man who has suffered. He has had to pay the penalty, and now he is being penalized again with this so-called temporary surtax on his income tax. What I would like to know from the Minister of Finance tonight is where and when these penalties stop? When does it become possible for a man to be rewarded for ambition and energy, rather than penalized? When does it become possible, realistic and practical for a man to be rewarded for being Canadian, for devoting his life's work and energies to the improvement of the state of society in this country, instead of being continually harassed from a financial point of view and subjected to penalties by a professional socialist undertaking?
I would like to move an amendment to clause 5 of the bill, but I understand, sir, it would be ruled out on technical grounds. Therefore I do not intend to move an amendment at this time, but I set myself firmly on record as being in steadfast opposition to this clause, and I am prepared to vote against it.
What we need in this country are tax incentives, not tax penalties as provided by this clause. Tax incentives are necessary as a means of increasing our productivity from coast to coast, both on an individual and on a collective level. Only if we increase our productivity will we find our way out of the morass into which we have stumbled under the present administration and its inept economic policies, policies which seem destined to lead us into fiscal disaster.
It pains me, on the strength of what I have said in the last few minutes and on the strength of my philosophical commitment as a Conservative, to support any measure put forward by the N.D.P., but I must say that I agree with the sentiments behind the amendment proposed earlier today by the hon. member for Broadview when he suggested the elimination of clause 5(l)(b), the requirement stipulating that $600 would be one of the brackets surrounding the new temporary surtax.
I support the sentiments behind that amendment, because I agree with the hon. member's argument that the prescription in the clause as now worded militates most severely against the small wage earner. Actually it militates against all wage earners, but I had admitted in my earlier statements this
Income Tax Act
evening that there are some Canadians to whom the additional surtax would not be so great a financial burden. However, the people with whom I am most concerned are those in the lower and medium income brackets, to whom it would be a great financial burden.
That is why I, despite the philosophical conflict I have to overcome in my own mind, do support the sentiments behind the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Broadview, because he has put his finger on the nub of the difficulty, the nub of the weakness, the flaw and the unfairness of this legislation, namely that it militates most severely against the man who is the backbone of this country, the small and medium sized wage earner, with a home and family that he has to support and children he has to feed and educate. I must say that I found the entire speech of the hon. member for Broadview a refreshing return to sanity, after the remarks made earlier in the afternoon by his colleague, the hon. member for Sudbury.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Like many other members in this chamber I felt that the remarks of the hon. member for Sudbury represented the most outrageous socialistic polemics I have had heard in this house since I came here. I am given to believe that many members, with much greater seniority in this chamber than I, would argue that it was the most outrageous dissertation of an unsupportable nature in the area of socialism and left wing thinking they have ever heard in the years they have been in the house. So, it was extremely gratifying to me to hear a voice of sanity come from that comer of the chamber in the person of the hon. member for Broadview. I reiterate my support for the sentiments contained in his amendment.
In a final reference to the contribution made from that corner of the chamber I should like to say that the remarks delivered by the hon. member for Sudbury represented to me a dredging up of some of the most hoary old chestnuts of socialism and left wing politics. His party could not get anyone to swallow those chestnuts in the past and will not have any success now. The hon. member for Sudbury no doubt is still convinced that it is practical to peddle them, but I doubt that he will have much success in his attempted sale of such outrageous ideas.
It is admitted that the nation is in a fiscal financial situation which requires financial and economic assistance where the federal purse is concerned. But there are many

February 15, 1968
Income Tax Act
sources available from which to obtain the money, without going to the oppressive extreme of levying this kind of unsavoury penalty on the middle and low wage earners of Canada who form the majority of the people of this country. There are two areas of public spending to which members from this and other parties have referred in the debate today. I should like to refer to the speech of the hon. member for Perth and also that of the hon. member for Villeneuve. I would also cite the current example of Hon. Lionel Chevrier, who I understand is on a tour of the French speaking nations of Africa, investigating the extent to which we as a nation might participate in external aid to those countries.
I have no quarrel with any exercise in external aid to any countries in the world of any political or ethnic extraction or persuasion. However, I would simply like to ask the Minister of Finance and his colleagues why we expand our contributory function in areas of this type, when on the other hand in order to raise the necessary money to keep the economy turning we must levy additional penalties on the taxpayers of Canada. This has been my experience every year since I came here a little over two years ago. Surely economic charity should begin here at home in Canada. Before we attempt to expand ourselves too far into these other areas of finance and fiscal support we should think of financial fiscal support and relief for our wage earners and taxpayers in Canada. I see no justification for the kind of spending to which I have just referred, and the kind of public spending which is projected for example for the immediate future in the Ottawa area. I see no justification for this, when we turn around and levy additional taxes and penalties on the hard pressed wage earners, pensioners, widows, elderly and retired persons of this country.
In his remarks earlier today the hon. member for Villeneuve spoke with scorn about the terminology used in clause 5. He referred to the words "temporary surtax" and suggested that they were a sham. In the lifetime of this government there is nothing in the field of taxation that is temporary. This is about as temporary as the location of the national capital here in Ottawa. This is a permanent addition to our tax burden, and there should be no attempt to dissemble that fact before the hard pressed wage earners and taxpayers of this country who will have to supply the money this government has run out of.

I have cited some exercises in the general area of public expenditure which I feel are inadvisable in the light of the steps the government is taking here in the form of this income tax surtax. There are two or three other exercises which could be added. One is the expense of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, which I find in my part of the country, and in other parts of the country which I have visited, has outraged most people who are knowledgeable about the work of the commission and the amount of money it is costing the taxpayers of Canada. This no doubt is a very worth-while study, but is it as worth-while as the stabilization of the financial life of this country would be?
I suggest that expenditures of this type should be deferred or postponed, at this time when public money is so short that the taxpayers are being asked to make up the deficit, until the time arrives when public money is available as a result of the general productivity of the nation. I suggest that this surtax will have precisely the opposite effect on the economy of this country to that which the Minister of Finance hoped to achieve through its implementation. I suggest that it will force people to cut back on their purchases and participate less in the exercise of oiling the machinery of the economy of this country. They will tend to participate less in the general function of keeping the economy moving, alive, energetic, productive and progressive. I suggest further that the effect of this type of slow-down and cut-back will be so serious that I would not attempt to give a prognosis at this time. I believe the effect of that cutback and slow-down would be serious enough to merit a separate full scale debate in this chamber.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance that he think back to the thirties, when there was a cry from those who were on relief which could be heard across this land. I submit to the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the government that today across Canada from coast to coast it is not the cry of those who are on relief which can be heard, but the cry of those who seek relief from the oppression of the cost-price-tax squeeze in which they have been caught for the past four years.

Mr. Chairman, as a member who represents to a very large degree the type of citizen who it has been suggested has been carrying an unfair tax burden for many years, I feel it is incumbent upon me to take
February 15, 1968

strong exception to this proposal of the Minister of Finance, which would perpetuate and add to the injustices that now prevail in our present tax laws. I should say in passing that I was very happy to hear that the hon. member for Winnipeg South recognizes the voice of sanity in our ranks. It is very evident from the speeches this afternoon that one will not hear a similar voice in the area to our right.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
We have been told that there are two things we can be sure of on this earth; death and taxes.
And Liberals.

I would be the first to agree that taxes are necessary. If we accept and expect services we must pay for them, and there is only one way to pay-through taxes. The government has a responsibility to see that taxes are levied on an equitable basis. It is in this respect that the government of today and previous governments have failed miserably. I do not pretend to be an expert on economics or monetary and fiscal policy and, like the hon. member for Winnipeg South, I intend to stay away from a discussion of that side of the coin. Some of my colleagues have done an admirable job in presenting our feelings in respect of economic aspects.
Surely no one will contradict me when I say that governments from the municipal level, up, are trying to high heaven to find additional finances. Municipalities in particular are having a very difficult time to finance their operations. I attended a meeting in a mining municipality in northern Ontario not long ago. The paramount concern of this group of people was that not enough revenue from the mining industry was being returned to the municipality to cover the cost of providing municipal services and educational needs. The only suggestion this group could make was that it should pressure the province into providing more financial assistance.
Who would pay for this increased assistance provided for northern municipalities by Queen's Park? This money must come from the same source, the taxpayers. The taxpayer, as has been suggested by the Carter commission and others, has been overburdened through taxes. We can solve nothing until we establish a new tax base. There is no point in transferring tax imposition from one place to another, because in the long run the taxes come from the same source.

I found something else which was of interest when I attended that meeting, namely the minutes of a previous meeting. They had passed a motion opposing the recommendations of the Carter commission dealing with the elimination of withholding tax and depletion allowances regarding mining and oil companies. I can only suggest that the municipality was panicked into taking this stand because of threats on the part of these companies. This is understandable, because these municipalities are totally dependant on the income from the production and primary processing of natural resources or raw materials. I am sure they felt that the adoption of these Carter commission recommendations would result in the destruction of their economies.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Has he read the Carter commission report?
I have read the summary, sir.
Does he believe the recommendations should be implemented in their entirety?

I know exactly what the hon. member has in mind. If mining companies and insurance companies paid the taxes they should be paying the tax rate for the average individual would be much lower. It would not make much difference to these companies, if these recommendations were implemented.
Do you believe that all the recommendations of the report should be implemented?

I think perhaps there should be some modification in certain areas, but I do not intend to identify those areas. If Kenneth Carter did anything, he emphasized the fact that too many have been getting a free ride for too long. Unless these recommendations are implemented and unless we develop a new tax base, the greater proportion of taxes will still come from that group of people who are now overly tax burdened.
Let me comment briefly on the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West in respect of corporation taxes. There is more than one kind of corporation. We have many small corporations, with as many financial

difficulties as have the wage earners. These corporations do not wield any great power. There are other corporations, to which I have alluded, which greatly influence our economy. To a great extent they control economic factors. I suspect that some of these corporations hold our governments in the palms of their hands.
It was interesting to note that immediately after the Carter commission recommendations became public our desks were covered with briefs and submissions from members of that 5 per cent of our population who exercise this control. It is time the voice of the other 95 per cent was heard.
We have often heard from members sitting on the front benches across the way about our high standard of living and our affluent society. I am the first to agree that our wage earners are living in nice, modern homes with all, or most, available appliances. They are living quite comfortably. The thing that has escaped the attention of most people is that this affluent society picture is a myth. Even though these people are living in modern homes, and even though they enjoy comfortable lives with a reasonable amount of security, they live from pay day to pay day. I speak with some authority in this regard because I spent most of my lifetime working among these people. I am not being critical of this situation or the people who live in this way; but it is only because of credit buying that they at this time enjoy a reasonably comfortable life. But the fact still remains that their security begins and ends with the pay cheque. If anything happens to the pay cheque, if a person becomes unemployed, the security finishes, the home is lost and, in many cases, a good portion of what is in the home also disappears.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
My colleagues have referred to the discriminatory aspects of tax exemption. They have referred to the need of exemption for tools, clothing, etc., which are a necessity in most cases for these people in their mode of employment. I believe there is another matter to be considered in this respect, namely the question of transportation expenses. In this day and age it is a practical impossibility for any employee to live within a short distance of his place of employment. He is practically forced to live 10, 20, 30 or even 40 miles from where he is employed. This is particularly true of the area from which I come. As a result, transportation costs take a great bite

out of the pay cheque of the employee; yet they cannot under any circumstances claim exemption for transportation expenses.
Another example of this was brought to my attention recently. I refer to the situation of professional fire fighters. I believe this matter comes within the jurisdiction of the emergency measures act. These people are compelled by law to be available to go anywhere within reason in case of emergency. Penalties are involved if they do not go to the place of emergency; and if they do not go, they must have a very good excuse for not going.
However, Mr. Chairman, there is no provision for the transportation of these people. In the case of dire emergency they are sometimes required to travel great distances. In some cases, in order not to violate the law they must have transportation, usually by means of a car, and they must keep up the insurance on the automobile, and so on. I believe this is another very glaring example of where tax exemptions should be provided. While wage earners are having this difficulty, we find there are those who claim exemptions for wining and dining and living high on the hog, so to speak. This is one of the things that very much bothers the average working man.
With regard to the tax holidays for mining corporations, as far as I am concerned I do not think they are necessary; in fact I would class them as an evil. But in addition to this, I think the minister should take a long look to see whether there are not abuses of the exemptions already provided. I suggest this is a matter well worth looking into. It appears to me that some of these exemptions go far beyond what should reasonably be considered as applicable.
As far as depletion allowances are concerned, I think it is a sad commentary on our whole economic process when large companies are granted depletion allowances for depleting expendable resources that, after all, are the heritage of every Canadian citizen.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like once again to prevail upon the minister to take a serious look at the tax policy of the government and the effect it is having on the average Canadian citizen. I believe the time is long overdue when we should come up with something entirely different in the way of a tax base. It is high time that the 95 per cent of this nation who suffer from our tax policy were given a little consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I should not like this

opportunity to pass without giving the minister the benefit of my advice, which he has never taken in the past. I should also like to refer to some of the minister's statements when he introduced this rather disastrous budget. It may be a little unkind on February 15, 1968, to quote what the minister said on November 30, 1967, as appears at page 4901 of Hansard. Here is our Minister of Finance looking in his clear, crystal ball with regard to the future. He has a somewhat different role than I have. Mine is a rather invidious one. I have never got much satisfaction out of being able to say, "I told you so", because Cassandra was never the go-go girl of the party. However, there is a contrast in the views expressed by the minister and those which I expressed a few days later. This is what the minister said when introducing his budget on November 30:
Looking ahead, in 1968 a somewhat greater increase in production than this year in real terms and a somewhat smaller increase in prices is indicated. This appraisal anticipates a revival in economic activity in the United States and a continuation of growth in production in Europe and Japan, all important markets for us. Consequently, I expect to see a resumption in the growth of our exports. We can certainly expect a continuing increase in the expenditures of Canadian consumers, probably at a greater rate than this year. Housing expenditures can be expected to rise next year. Mortgage funds should be more readily available as a result of the more flexible interest rates on insured mortgages as well as a reduction in the competition for funds and the entry of the banks into the market this year. Already, as hon. members know, there has been a very substantial increase.
Alas-
Who said that?
Oh, it was a Pollyanna, the Minister of Finance. But perhaps the sun was shining brightly on November 30 and it was not until the middle of February, 1968, that the frost of reality came down.

Really, Mr. Chairman, I wonder that the minister can sit here and have the effrontery to say this, when we have heard of the great number of people in Canada who are desperately in need of housing. These people require mortgage funds, which are not available. Interest rates are continuing to rise. The other day, when I pointed out the effect of the sharp increase in interest rates, the minister considered that it was a matter of so little consequence that he had not even spoken to the banks or suggested to them, apparently, that this was not in accordance with the prognostications he had made at the time we had the revision of the Bank Act.
1 suggest that when he told us there would be a somewhat greater increase in production this year he must have forgotten that in a moment of rashness when he introduced the budget he said there would be a slight decline in production. He told us this was necessary in order that we control inflation. If the minister does not remember that, he had better look at his speech of November 30, when he said he was looking forward to a slight decline in production, regrettably, but because of the economic situation he felt this would take place.
Quite apart from this, Mr. Chairman, I think this bill contains fundamental implications that are much more important than the 5 per cent surtax on income, which we say is merely the revelation of the bankruptcy of this government's policies. This government has several obsessions. One is the necessity of maintaining simultaneously two contradictory and incompatible policies which tie their hands, and have tied their hands steadily for some time. The minister laughs. I can assure him the people of Canada are not laughing. I can assure him, too, that the economists in Canada are not laughing. I am so tired of economists coming to me, as if I were responsible, and saying to me: Is that man Sharp crazy? I say: I do not think so; what is he doing? I have to say I am not a miracle worker, so I cannot unscrew the inscrutable. If the minister thinks the individuals of this nation support him, then I suspect he will find the answer on April 6, because there will be a lot of people telling the delegates to the convention that they have been talking to businessmen who are not in support of the Minister of Finance.

There is only one way in which the minister can reach the objective which he told us he wanted to reach, namely to contain inflation and at the same time expand and develop the growth of our economy. However, he will not take it. He turned a deaf ear to the suggestions we made to him about the incompatibility of his policy of maintaining a fixed exchange rate and at the same time maintaining a ceiling on exchange reserves. This is continually causing him trouble.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is only one way in which we can reduce interest rates. There is only one way in which we can expand the economy and that is by taking action to do so. When the minister is tied to the necessity of maintaining the dollar at 92.5, when he is tied to the necessity of keeping our exchange reserves below a certain ceiling, then he is unable to expand the economy. Instead of that, he contracts it; and he admits himself he is contracting the economy. The steps he took were designed to contract the economy. The words he used, of course, were the euphemistic ones of allowing a little slack to develop in the economy. This is not a phrase, Mr. Chairman, that will appeal to those who are the victims of that slack, because in order to be effective there must be a decline in employment; there must be a contraction of the economy. There must be an increase in interest rates. Of course this reduction is being deliberately pushed at the present time.
Because of the position of this government, Canada's future depends on a continual inflow of capital from outside. In spite of that fact, Mr. Chairman, more and more informed voices are being raised in Canada expressing great anxiety with regard to the out-flow of capital from Canada. On December 8 I quoted from a release by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. Apparently the minister did not either read my speech or consult the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, so I will just put it on the record again. The quotation is from a current review of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, which reads as follows:
Canada's current account deficit with the United States in the second quarter of 1967 (excluding gold production available for export which is conventionally attributed to the United States account) was $544 million. Net capital movements between the two countries produced an inflow of $58 million as an influx of $239 million of long term capital was in part offset by an outflow on shortterm account of $181 million.
Now, again and again in recent months we have been hearing the statements of financial
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands).!
analysts who tell us in effect that we are getting almost nothing in the way of net inflow of capital. It is balanced by the outflows. The minister, however, still persists in going to New York and praying for the stability of United States markets, because he feels that will preserve our economy. He begs them to continue the inflow of capital here which will be offset by what is going out on account of previous inflows. I suggest to the minister that eventually he will have to take some steps to expand the Canadian economy to reverse the trend toward rising unemployment and rising prices, by accepting not my advice but the advice of competent economist after competent economist throughout the country. They say he should seek to return to the floating exchange rate and seek to stem the outflow, to control the inflow of capital from abroad and permit the Canadian economy to develop in the way in which our resources would certainly warrant.
I have wondered, Mr. Chairman, just why the minister took the action he did, because he told us he was going to control inflation. At the same time he told us that he knew quite well the inflation was not the usual, classical, too much money chasing too few goods, and obviously he could not sustain that idea. Nowhere could he point to a shortage of goods. On the other hand, he said it was the cost-push type of inflation. What does he do? He takes the idiotic step, the ineffective step which, if designed to do nothing more than control the classical type of inflation, would be an ineffective one. He puts on his 5 per cent surtax on income, which is a nuisance to a lot of people. This measure according to his own estimate, is only going to bring in $185 million. He increased the tax on liquor and tobacco, which is only going to bring in $95 million. He is going to get corporations to advance their tax payments so he will get them a little sooner than otherwise; but this is a one shot affair.
Then the minister tells us that the total tax yield for 1968-69 will be $9,700 million and expenditures will be $10,300 million, with a deficit of $600 million. In the light of the fact that the other day the President of the Treasury Board uncautiously promised this parliament the government was going to balance the budget next year, I would have thought the minister would have taken more decisive steps if he felt that this type of inflation could be controlled by withdrawing purchasing power from the hands of the people. Instead of that, he does not even withdraw enough

money to make any difference. He takes no steps whatever to control the actual excess of inflation at the present time.
I do not know how long ago it is, Mr. Chairman, but it must be about six weeks ago that we asked the minister if he was going to investigate the rise in the prices of copper and nickel. He assured us he was going to look into it. Subsequently, when we have asked him, he has still been looking into it but he has not done anything about it. We have not heard anything from him about the famous guide lines that were going to prevent these unseemly and completely unjustifiable price increases which of course enter into all other costs and add to the inflationary pressures.
He does not do anything on that side. Instead of that, he takes away a bit of purchasing power, but more important still he creates unemployment. No matter what the minister's brave words of November 30 may have been, or his equally rash, brave words tonight, he has made it almost impossible for people in Canada of medium or even fairly sizeable incomes to build houses today.

HEALTH AND WELFARE-MEASURES TO COMBAT PROBLEMS CAUSED BY ALCOHOLISM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I attempted to raise on the orders of the day the question whether the government was considering doing anything more with regard to the very important health and welfare problem caused by alcoholism in Canada. Mr. Speaker ruled the question out of order, so I have of course availed myself of this evening's late sitting to bring the matter up again. In support of the importance of the matter I hope in a very few minutes to put some facts on the record.
There can be no question at all that alcoholism causes, and has caused for a great many years, grave damage to the health and welfare of individuals, to families and to the state. Also in these days it carries with it modern problems, such as those evidenced by the fact that 50 per cent of fatal automobile collisions are caused by people who have taken alcohol to an extent far beyond the normal. This one instance alone, namely the toll taken by alcoholism in traffic accidents, accounts for hundreds of preventable deaths in Canada every 12 months, thousands of preventable casualties and millions of preventable economic losses.
I have cited this one particular aspect of the toll taken by alcoholism in Canada, but this is only one part of the whole sad story. There are also countless broken homes and marriages both in this city and throughout Canada as a result of alcoholism. We all know this is so. My question is: What is the government, and specifically the Department of National Health and Welfare, doing to help those people, and organizations that are actively engaged in trying to combat this evil?
As some hon. members know, I-and there are other members as well-have for years urged that the federal government and all other governments do something to combat the evils of cigarette addiction. I am pleased to commend the government for having done something to combat smoking. It has not done enough but it has done something to help prevent diseases such as lung cancer, heart trouble, emphysema and so on.
