But, Mr. Speaker, what is the government doing about the problem of alcohol, a problem that is growing? The latest figures indicate that while the federal government raised revenue in excess of $275 million in the last fiscal year from the sale of alcoholic beverages, it contributed nothing, or nothing material, to any anti-alcoholism or temperance program in Canada. Why not? Surely this is a field in which there is a national problem of health and welfare. This problem has seen the emergence of different organizations at the provincial level and at the semipublic federal level who devote their efforts to solving the problem of alcohol.
For example, the pamphlet which is put out by the Canadian Federation on Alcohol Problems says that the purposes of the federation are to bring about enlightenment and understanding with regard to alcoholic problems and, generally, to do everything possible to improve the lot of those suffering from this cause. The organization is national and has the support of such organizations as the Anglican Church of Canada, the Canadian Baptist Church, the Pentecostal Church, the Presbyterian Church, the Roman Catholic Church, Seventh-Day Adventists and the United Church of Canada. I think that the government should consider augmenting the work that is done by these bodies.
Since the government derives a revenue of approximately $275 million a year from the sale of alcohol and since excessive use of such alcohol brings about disease, social problems, an increase in crime, increasing traffic accidents, and so on, would the government not consider seriously devoting a small part of its annual multimillion dollar revenue to meeting the problem of alcoholics? I suggest that the government consider allocating one half of one per cent of that revenue every year to aid in the work being undertaken by this federation.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Margaret Rideout (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-MEASURES TO COMBAT PROBLEMS CAUSED BY ALCOHOLISM
speechtext:
As stated in this house on January 23, 1968, and as reported in Hansard at page 5900, the Department of National Health and Welfare has no specific program on this subject but has assisted provinces in a variety of ways for many years. For the general co-ordination carried out by the Canadian Foundation on Alcoholism, a grant of $15,000 is made annually.
The problems of the alcoholic are indeed matters of real concern to the individual, his


or her family, and to all who come in contact with them. Alcoholism is primarily a personal problem, and must be combated at the personal, family and local level. It has however, a relationship to crime, traffic accidents and to costly health and welfare programs that receive public concern.
In recognizing this situation, the Department of National Health and Welfare is at all times ready to consider requests from provinces for assistance with research or services that seek to diminish or prevent the problems of alcohol. In addition to this provincial interest, the department keeps under continuing review the available statistics and other information on this subject, with a view to formulating whatever co-ordinating effort may seem likely to be effective.

Mr. Speaker, earlier this week I asked the Minister of Agriculture a question about possible long term government loans to fair boards and exhibition companies, for the construction of multipurpose buildings and facilities which would be suitable for local fairs. Mr. Speaker ruled that the question was not urgent; yet, with due respect, I do consider that question urgent and therefore I bring it up again at this time. I might explain that by "multipurpose buildings" I meant exhibition buildings that could be used for community purposes all year around.
The urgency of the question arises from this. Plans for summer fairs and exhibitions must be made now and if building loans are to be available this year the minister should announce that immediately.

I wish to put on record why fair boards and exhibition companies have the right to expect loans to be granted. In June, 1965, in answer to my question, the then minister of agriculture, Hon. Harry Hays, stated as reported in Votes and Proceedings of June 4, 1965:
The development of a program of long-term loans to exhibitions for major construction programs is presently under consideration.
On December 14, 1966, the present minister answered a letter I had sent regarding exhibition loans. Here is the last paragraph of his letter:
The Government, as you indicated, has under consideration a program of long-term loans. I am

hopeful that we can move forward on such a plan within a reasonable period. However, you will appreciate that this will take legislative action and as soon as a decision has been reached an announcement will be made.

Perhaps I may review briefly what has happened. It is probable that if this system had not been discontinued we would still be providing this type of assistance to agricultural societies.
